43063491.title: Serplulimab combined with nab-paclitaxel and epirubicin in high-risk, early HR+/HER2- breast cancer (HELEN-B 018): a multicentre, single-arm, phase 2 trial.
43063491.author: Dai H
43063491.abstract:
PURPOSE: This phase 2 trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of serplulimab combined with nab-paclitaxel and epirubicin in high-risk, early HR+/HER2- breast cancer NCT06394661 Patients and Methods: This multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 trial was conducted in China at 6 hospitals. Patients were eligible if they were 18 years or older, with early HR+/HER2- breast cancer (T1c N1-3 or T2-4 any N), and Ki-67 ≥20%. Participants received intravenous nab-paclitaxel (260 mg/m2) plus intravenous epirubicin (75 mg/m2) on day 1, and intravenous serplulimab (4.5 mg/kg) on day 3 of the treatment cycle, every 3 weeks for 6 cycles. The primary outcome was the rate of pCR (defined as ypT0/is ypN0), assessed in the full analysis set.
RESULTS: 101 participants started trial treatment and were included in the full analysis set. pCR was achieved in 23 patients (22.8%, 95% CI 15.3%-32.4%). RCB 0 or 1 was achieved in 34 patients (33.7%, 95% CI 24.8%-43.8%). The pCR rate was higher in PD-L1-positive (combined positive score (CPS)≥1) tumors (44.4%, 95% CI 30.0%-59.9%) than in PD-L1-negative tumors (5.4%, 95% CI 1.4%-15.8%, P <0.001). During the neoadjuvant phase, 30 (29.7%) patients experienced grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events. No new safety signals were identified and there were no treatment-related deaths.
CONCLUSIONS: Serplulimab combined with nab-paclitaxel and epirubicin showed anti-tumor activity and manageable safety in patients with HR+/HER2- breast cancer, and the pCR rate was higher in PD-L1-positive tumors. These findings support further evaluation of this regimen in randomized controlled trials.

43063490.title: A randomised phase II trial of neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without concurrent aromatase inhibitor therapy in ER-positive breast cancer (ANZ1401 ELIMINATE).
43063490.author: Murray N
43063490.abstract:
PURPOSE: Patients with large estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, HER2-negative breast cancers have low pathologic complete response (pCR) rates with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. We aimed to determine the rate of tumor downstaging with concurrent neoadjuvant chemo-endocrine therapy (CET) compared with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (CT) in clinical stage 2/3 breast cancer.
METHODS: This phase II trial randomized women with operable grade 2-3, ER+/HER2- tumors with a primary >20mm 2:1 to neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus concurrent letrozole, or chemotherapy alone. Primary outcome was proportion of tumors down-staged to ≤20mm and ypT0-1ypN0/stage 0-1A. Evaluation of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), RNA and DNA sequencing were performed to identify correlates of response.
RESULTS: ELIMINATE randomized 134 women, with 122 evaluable for the primary outcome. 24% (19/81) with CET and 20% (8/41) with CT (difference 3.9%, 95% CI -11% to 19%) achieved downstaging to ypT0-1ypN0. Overall, 6/122 (5%) had a pCR, all in the CET arm. MRI response was seen in 79% (CET), 66% (CT). Considering grade 3 tumors, 5/22 (23%) in the CET arm and 0/10 in the CT arm achieved pCR. Translational analyses revealed that pCR and RCB 0-I responses were enriched in baseline tumors with higher grade, higher TILs, elevated TMB, and immune activation signatures, independently of treatment arm.
CONCLUSION: CET did not significantly increase downstaging to stage 0-IA. Exploratory analyses suggest a subset of high-grade ER+/HER2- tumors enriched for immune activity, with elevated TILs and high TMB, were associated with favourable response irrespective of treatment assignment. These findings support further exploration of immune-genomic biomarkers in future studies of ER+/HER2- breast cancer.

43058942.title: FDA Approves Giredestrant for Advanced Breast Cancer.
43058942.abstract: The FDA approved giredestrant in combination with everolimus for ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer based on the results of the phase III evERA trial. In addition, the agency authorized the FoundationOne Liquid CDx assay for assessing ESR1 status to determine who would benefit from this treatment regimen.

43039016.title: Genome-directed treatment targets and mutational signature biomarkers: a retrospective, pan-solid tumour analysis.
43039016.author: Black D
43039016.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The clinical application of precision oncology therapies is currently restricted to selected cancer cases harbouring highly specific mutations. Targeted therapies are typically approved for use in specific tumour types in which these alterations occur frequently. We aimed to systematically catalogue targetable alterations and genome-wide biomarkers across all solid tumour types to identify additional therapeutic opportunities.
METHODS: In this retrospective, pan-solid tumour analysis, for the primary cancer cohort, we used matched fresh frozen tumour and normal DNA samples and anonymised patient metadata from a discovery cohort of 11 013 tumours comprising 19 tumour types collected from 10 334 participants in the UK-based 100 000 Genomes Project (100kGP). Participants were recruited to this cohort through 13 National Health Service Genomic Medicine Centres or hospitals affiliated to the 100kGP between 2012 and 2019. For the metastatic cancer cohort, we used matched tumour and normal DNA samples and anonymised patient metadata from a cohort of 6016 solid tumours collected from 5658 patients from the Netherlands who contributed to the Hartwig Medical Foundation (HMF) database (accessed Aug 19, 2025). Snap-frozen tumour DNA and matched normal DNA from blood samples underwent whole-genome sequencing. Potentially targetable alterations, comprising (1) immediately actionable alterations, (2) investigational alterations, and (3) mutational signature-informed features, were sought in all samples. The primary outcome of this study was to assess the pan-cancer frequency and tissue distribution of potentially targetable alterations.
FINDINGS: Between July 1, 2025, and March 3, 2026, we analysed samples from 17 029 tumours from the 100kGP and HMF cohorts. Immediately actionable alterations were identified in 2081 (18·9%) of 11 013 primary and 1559 (25·9%) of 6016 metastatic cancers; a further 1204 (10·9%) primary and 867 (14·4%) metastatic cancers harboured investigational alterations or mutational signature-informed features. 2914 (51·1%) of the 5706 immediately actionable variants identified were found in tumour types where the biomarker is not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. Although some immediately actionable alterations (including gene-fusion targets and MET exon 14 skipping variants) were restricted to fewer tumour types, most immediately actionable alterations (including HER2 amplification, RAS-RAF pathway alterations, IDH1 mutations, and DNA repair deficiencies) occurred across multiple tumour types, frequently beyond those for which matched targeted therapies are currently approved. Mutational-signature biomarkers of DNA repair or replication deficiencies were similarly observed across tumour types. Metastatic cancers, including rare and moderately rare tumour types and cancers of unknown primary, harboured a notably high prevalence and diversity of targetable events.
INTERPRETATION: Our findings support comprehensive whole-genome sequencing assessment of cancers irrespective of tumour type. Prospective clinical trials are required to establish whether therapeutic vulnerabilities identified by whole-genome sequencing can extend the effective use of targeted therapies beyond their current tumour-specific indications.
FUNDING: Cancer Research UK, Breast Cancer Research Foundation, National Institute for Health and Care Research, Jeffrey Cheah Foundation.

43063371.title: Reach of State-Mandated Insurance Coverage for Fertility Preservation in Patients With Cancer.
43063371.author: Chacón KM
43063371.abstract:
PURPOSE: Fertility preservation (FP) before cancer treatment effectively reduces iatrogenic infertility. Twenty-three states and the District of Columbia have passed insurance mandates for medically indicated FP coverage, but empiric data on population reach are lacking. We assessed the reach of California's mandate among young patients with cancer and sought to identify if social determinants of health (SDOH) are associated with mandate eligibility.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted of all female patients age 0-42 years and male patients age 0-49 years newly diagnosed with cancer at a National Cancer Institute-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center between 2021 and 2024. SDOH included sex, age, race, ethnicity, primary language, and Social Vulnerability Index (SVI). The primary outcome was eligibility for FP coverage under California's mandate. Secondary outcomes included insurer confirmation of FP benefits and time required for benefit verification.
RESULTS: Of 903 patients, 18% were eligible for state-mandated FP benefits. Ineligibility was due to insurance by Medicaid (49%), ineligible commercial plans (37%), military-based plans (9%), federal-employee plans (2%), or being uninsured (3%). Non-English-speaking patients were 64% less likely to be eligible versus English-speaking patients (adjusted relative risk, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.17 to 0.75]) in adjusted analysis. Subgroup analyses showed that eligible patients differed significantly from ineligible Medicaid-insured patients by race, primary language, and SVI, but did not differ from ineligible commercially insured patients. Among patients with plans subject to the mandate, insurers inaccurately reported that they had no FP coverage 28% of the time. Benefit verification required a median of 45 minutes per patient (range, 9-350 minutes, interquartile range, 25-80). These secondary outcomes differed significantly by insurer (P < .001).
CONCLUSION: California's mandate excludes most at-risk patients with cancer and perpetuates disparities in access. Future work in oncofertility health policy must consider mandate design and downstream implementation to eliminate barriers to care.

43045792.title: Global landscape of early-onset breast cancer: from understanding risk to precision prevention and cancer interception.
43045792.author: Wu S
43045792.abstract: Early-onset breast cancer (EOBC), defined in this Review as breast cancer diagnosed before 50 years of age, accounts for a growing proportion of global breast cancer incidence and is associated with disproportionately unfavourable outcomes. Although inherited susceptibility contributes to EOBC risk, the rising incidence and persistent disparities that characterize EOBC cannot be explained by genetics alone; molecular subtype distribution, modifiable exposures and healthcare-related factors also affect presentation, response to treatment and outcomes. In this Review, we synthesize epidemiological trends, providing an overview of the inherited and multifactorial risk determinants, tumour subtype distributions and modifiable exposures that shape EOBC across populations. We examine why age-based screening paradigms do not fully capture EOBC risk and discuss approaches to risk-informed early detection and diagnosis, emphasizing the need for prompt histopathological confirmation and biomarker-guided care. We then address structural and healthcare-related barriers that constrain implementation of such an approach, including diagnostic capacity, pathology infrastructure, treatment affordability and financial toxicity. Finally, we propose a roadmap for the prevention, early diagnosis and interception of EOBC that integrates family history, germline testing, ancestry-aware risk models, pathology, treatment access and resource-stratified implementation. We argue that biological risk architecture must be aligned with healthcare systems that translate risk recognition into prompt, equitable and optimal management, including appropriately adapted treatment, ultimately improving outcomes for patients with EOBC.

43044086.title: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures Used for Clinical Assessment in Adults Across the National Cancer Institute Community Oncology Research Program Practices.
43044086.author: Cooley ME
43044086.abstract:
PURPOSE: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) have been used to monitor patient response during cancer treatment and have resulted in improved clinical outcomes. This study examined the use of PROMs implemented for clinical assessment across the National Cancer Institute Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP) community practices.
METHODS: This study used data from the 2017 and 2022 NCORP cancer care delivery landscape surveys. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze survey item data. Logistic regression models examined the relationship between geographic region and the organizational characteristics of practice settings that used and recorded PROMS in the electronic health record (EHR).
RESULTS: Although most practices routinely assessed distress in 2017 (87.8%) and 2022 (91.1%), only 32.1% of practices used PROMs aimed at assessing health-related quality of life (HRQOL) or symptoms in 2017 and the rate decreased in 2022 (23.2%). A wide variety of questionnaires were used to measure distress and HRQOL/symptoms. No geographic or organizational factors were associated with use of PROMs for distress, whereas practices in the West and those with lower cancer patient volume were less likely to use PROMs to assess HRQOL or symptoms. Geographic location and participation in the Oncology Care Model (OCM) were associated with recording distress screening PROMs in the EHR, whereas participation in the OCM was the only factor associated with recording HRQOL or symptom assessment PROMs.
CONCLUSION: Given that most adults with cancer are treated in their communities, it is critical to gain a better understanding of the factors associated with the low use of PROMs for HRQOL/symptom assessment in community-based practices. Alternative models for collecting PROMs may be needed to minimize future inequities in patient-centered cancer care delivery.

43044082.title: Most Chemotherapy Administration Sites Are Rural: Evidence From the Minnesota All-Payer Claims Database and a Framework for State-Level Cancer Care Surveillance.
43044082.author: Swenson W
43044082.abstract:
PURPOSE: Chemotherapy is widely assumed to be concentrated in urban cancer centers, but state-level data on its geographic distribution are limited. We used the Minnesota All-Payer Claims Database (MN APCD) to characterize rural and urban chemotherapy administration sites, assess quality certification rates, and present a replicable methodology for other states.
METHODS: Claims for carboplatin (J9045) and paclitaxel (J9264, J9267) from the 2022 MN APCD were analyzed. Chemotherapy administration sites were identified from billing claims, geolocated, and assigned Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes (urban: 1-3; rural: 4-10). Quality Oncology Practice Initiative (QOPI) certification and Commission on Cancer (CoC) accreditation were matched by facility. National QOPI (N = 217) and CoC (N = 1,093) data were analyzed by RUCA category for comparison.
RESULTS: Among 104 sites, 55 (52.9%) were rural, accounting for 10,117 (27.0%) of 37,526 claim lines. No rural site held QOPI certification (0% v 16.3% urban). Rural CoC accreditation was lower (25.5% v 42.9%). Nationally, rural practices comprised 14.7% of QOPI-certified sites and 13.4% of CoC-accredited programs, 15%-20% of the US population living in rural areas.
CONCLUSION: Despite published ASCO workforce data showing that only 7%-11.7% of medical oncologists practice in rural areas, 52.9% of Minnesota chemotherapy administration sites are rural, challenging the assumption that chemotherapy delivery is an urban and suburban phenomenon. Rural sites deliver 27.0% of claim volume, suggesting a broadly distributed but lower-intensity rural oncology infrastructure invisible to workforce-based mapping. This APCD-based framework is scalable and replicable; with approximately 25 states operating or developing mandatory APCDs, it can inform cancer control planning, direct resources to where care is delivered, and help close rural oncology disparities nationwide.

43035936.title: Home-Built environment as medicine for long-term cancer survivorship: a hard pill to prescribe.
43035936.author: Hernandez-Garcia E
43035936.abstract: Cancer survivorship is increasingly recognized as a chronic, accelerated aging-related state of health, with long-term care occurring largely within the community and home-built environment (H-BE)-the human-made or modified structures of the dwelling. Lifelong environmental exposures-such as fine particulate matter, circadian-disrupting light, and toxic chemicals-can exacerbate post-treatment inflammaging, disrupt resolution of inflammation, and shape trajectories of long-term outcomes. Yet patient-level H-BE interventions targeting these modifiable, non-lifestyle risk factors remain an overlooked clinical domain in survivorship research, clinical guidelines, and care delivery. In this Commentary, we present an evidence-based, living framework that positions the H-BE as an emerging, prescribable target for mitigating late toxicities, symptom burden, and their physiological precursors in aging cancer survivors. The framework is structured across eight Emerging Frontline Domains, interdependent capability areas to guide next-generation survivorship trials in the practice of H-BE as medicine and advance clinical translation primary care-level H-BE screening and dual clinical-environmental risk stratification; referral pathways and follow-up structures with BE health expertise; real-world characterization of H-BE exposure scenarios; drug-environment interaction mapping; shared mechanistic and biomarker-informed domains capturing inflammatory burden, inflammaging, and capacity to resolve inflammation; implementation technologies enabling longitudinal remote monitoring; and decentralized, adaptive and personalized trial designs to support scalable outpatient delivery. H-BE as medicine addresses a critical gap for middle-aged and older cancer survivors-those most affected by treatment-driven inflammaging, multimorbidity, and prolonged home exposure-and offers a mechanistically robust, actionable roadmap to advance H-BE interventions from research through feasibility testing into survivorship clinical practice.

43068431.title: EPHA2 and EPHB4 expression in human brain tumors and preclinical evaluation of EPHRIN-B2-based CAR-T cells.
43068431.author: Furui Y
43068431.abstract:
PURPOSE: To characterize EPHA2 and EPHB4 expression in human brain tumors and evaluate the preclinical antitumor activity of EPHRIN-B2-based chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells.
METHODS: EPHA2 and EPHB4 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry in 141 specimens from 116 patients; 113 specimens were included in analyses by histological category. EPHRIN-B2-based CAR-T cells were generated using the piggyBac transposon system. In vitro activity was evaluated against six brain tumor cell lines and a receptor-negative control line. Intracerebroventricular administration was assessed in two intracranial xenograft models, with mock T cells, control CAR-T cells, and phosphate-buffered saline as comparators.
RESULTS: EPHA2 expression was observed across histological categories, whereas higher EPHB4 expression was predominantly found in high-grade tumors. Among glioblastoma/gliosarcoma specimens, 74% and 37% had staining scores ≥ 2 for EPHA2 and EPHB4, respectively. High expression of both receptors within the same specimen was concentrated in high-grade tumors. CAR-T cells reduced viable tumor cell numbers and increased interferon-γ and interleukin-2 secretion against all six brain tumor cell lines, whereas no significant differences were detected with the receptor-negative control. Although differences from control T cells did not reach statistical significance, EPHRIN-B2-based CAR-T cells reduced tumor signals relative to saline-treated controls at selected time points in both xenograft models.
CONCLUSION: These findings characterize EPHA2 and EPHB4 expression in human brain tumors and demonstrate in vitro antitumor activity of EPHRIN-B2-based CAR-T cells, providing a basis for further studies to establish CAR-specific efficacy in intracranial tumors. REGISTRY AND THE REGISTRATION NO.
OF THE STUDY/TRIAL: N/A.

43063492.title: Molecularly profiling cell-free DNA from cerebrospinal fluid yields quantitative biomarkers to diagnose and monitor breast cancer leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.
43063492.author: Malani R
43063492.abstract:
PURPOSE: Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (LC), the spread of cancer to the fluid-filled spaces of the central nervous system, is an increasingly common and rapidly fatal complication of breast cancer. Standardized clinical diagnostic methods, such as cytology and MRI, have limited accuracy, do not identify therapy-defining mutations, and are not quantitative. Here, we sought to develop the molecular analysis of cell-free DNA in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as a quantitative tool to diagnose and monitor LC.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: Cell-free DNA from the CSF of 35 breast cancer patients referred for the clinical evaluation of potential LC underwent next-generation sequencing. TrueR sequencing, a duplex-based workflow, was used to suppress false positives during variant discovery. PolkaDot, a novel low-pass whole genome sequencing algorithm, quantitatively mapped genomic instability.
RESULTS: Twenty-three patients were clinically diagnosed with LC, and 12 patients were clinically determined not to have LC. TrueR somatic mutation detection was 78.3% sensitive and 100% specific for clinically confirmed LC and associated with worse overall survival (HR=9.5 [3.5-25.5], P=0.0003). PolkaDot was 87.0% sensitive and 100% specific and predicted worse overall survival (HR=17.5 [6.6-46.9], P=0.0001). Cytology (34.8% sensitive, 100% specific; HR=2.1 [0.6-7.6], P=0.15) and MRI (82.6% sensitive, 50.0% specific; HR=0.9 [0.3-2.5], P=0.76) were not prognostic. Using serial samples, the quantitative monitoring of the mutation molecular burden and genomic instability identified treatment susceptibility and resistance, and disease recurrence.
CONCLUSIONS: CSF cell-free DNA is a minimally invasive biomarker that provides an objective diagnosis of breast cancer LC and personalized molecular profiles for quantitative disease monitoring to support clinical management.

43062569.title: Stereotactic radiosurgery for locoregional leptomeningeal metastasis: defining a role for focal treatment.
43062569.author: Hajikarimloo B
43062569.abstract: Locoregional leptomeningeal metastasis, particularly discrete nodular recurrence after treatment of brain metastases, presents a therapeutic challenge distinct from diffuse leptomeningeal dissemination. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) may provide focal control of symptomatic or progressive nodules while limiting irradiation of uninvolved tissue. Available retrospective evidence supports feasibility and local radiographic response, but does not establish a survival benefit or protection against distant meningeal progression. Careful distinction among leptomeningeal nodules, dural seeding, and cavity recurrence is essential, as is assessment of the entire neuraxis and cerebrospinal fluid when appropriate. Patient selection should consider lesion distribution, neurologic function, prior irradiation, systemic disease control, and access to central nervous system-active therapies. Focal SRS should complement, rather than replace, comprehensive management of leptomeningeal disease. Prospective multicenter studies should prioritize neurologic function, distant meningeal progression, treatment burden, and patient-centered outcomes to define when local control yields meaningful clinical benefit. A multidisciplinary approach remains central to selecting treatment consistent with each patient's clinical goals.

43062499.title: Single-molecule whole-genome sequencing reveals genomic and epigenomic concordance between ultrasonic aspiration and surgical resection in meningioma: prospective feasibility series.
43062499.author: Unal M
43062499.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ultrasonic surgical aspirators, including Sonopet®, are widely used during skull base meningioma resection to enable safe tumor debulking in constrained corridors, but aspirated tumor fragments are often discarded. Whether this tissue supports genomic and epigenomic profiling comparable to standard resection tissue is unknown. The aim of this study was to determine whether Sonopet® aspirate is a viable substrate for long-read genomic and epigenomic profiling in skull base meningioma.
METHODS: We prospectively collected paired standard resection (R) and Sonopet® aspirate (S) specimens from seven patients with skull base meningioma and performed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read whole-genome sequencing using PromethION R10 flow cells. We compared sequencing yield, read quality, tumor purity, copy-number profiles, somatic single-nucleotide variant (SNV) burden, variant allele frequency, and CpG methylation between matched samples, then projected methylation profiles onto a reference framework of 121 EPIC array-profiled samples for molecular group classification.
RESULTS: Aspirates generated sequencing yields, read lengths, and tumor purity comparable to matched specimens. Copy-number profiles were largely concordant and recovered canonical meningioma alterations, with close agreement in total and loss burden (Lin's CCC = 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.00). SNV burden showed moderate agreement (CCC = 0.53, 95% CI - 0.28 to 0.99), with two discordant patients possibly reflecting intratumoral heterogeneity. Promoter methylation was closely correlated between pairs (Pearson r > 0.99 across ~ 177,000 promoters), and molecular group classification was concordant in all pairs except P1, where tumor purity was uncertain.
CONCLUSIONS: Sonopet® aspirate provides tissue comparable to standard resection specimens for long-read genomic and epigenomic profiling, supporting its use as a substrate for molecular diagnosis and translational research, particularly for subtotally resected tumors with limited tissue.

43056111.title: Pediatric Medical Imaging and Brain Tumor Risk.
43056111.author: Persiani F

43056070.title: Medical Imaging and Pediatric and Adolescent Brain Tumor Risk.
43056070.author: Miglioretti DL
43056070.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Ionizing radiation from medical imaging may increase brain tumor risk.
OBJECTIVE: To quantify brain tumor risk associated with radiation exposure from medical imaging in children and adolescents.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Retrospective cohort study of children born from 1996 through 2016 who were enrolled from birth in 6 US health care systems or Ontario, Canada, and were alive and cancer-free at age 2 years, with follow-up through December 31, 2017 (US sites), and December 31, 2024 (Ontario).
EXPOSURES: Cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging, lagged by 2 years.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Incident brain or other central nervous system tumors. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models for categorical dose, and excess relative risks (ERRs) were estimated using linear dose-response models for continuous dose.
RESULTS: Among 3 704 860 children (1 900 285 [51.3%] male) followed up for 45 671 641 person-years (mean follow-up, 12.3 years), 1536 brain tumors were diagnosed. Mean radiation dose from 1 head computed tomography (CT) examination was 66.2 mGy (SD, 22.2). Among children with cumulative dose of 1 mGy or greater, mean cumulative dose was 73 mGy (SD, 95) overall and 100 mGy (SD, 105) among those diagnosed with brain tumors. Compared with no exposure, brain tumor risk increased with cumulative dose (>0 to <1 mGy: HR, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.26]; 1 to <5 mGy: HR, 1.71 [95% CI, 0.88-2.96]; 5 to <50 mGy: HR, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.16-2.81]; 50 to <75 mGy: HR, 2.30 [95% CI, 1.64-3.12]; 75 to <100 mGy: HR, 2.02 [95% CI, 1.13-3.30]; 100 to <150 mGy: HR, 2.81 [95% CI, 1.53-4.66]; ≥150 mGy: HR, 3.85 [95% CI, 2.43-5.75]). Cumulative dose was associated with brain tumor risk overall (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.27 [95% CI, 0.83-1.77]; P < .001), with stronger associations for aggressive histologies (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.51 [95% CI, 1.00-2.11]; P < .001). By age 21 years, exposure comparable to 1 head CT was associated with 7.9 excess brain tumors per 10 000 children, or approximately 1 excess tumor per 1266 head CT examinations. The estimated population-attributable fraction was 10.1% (95% CI, 5.8%-14.2%).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Medical imaging in children and adolescents was associated with a dose-related increase in brain tumor risk. These findings support careful clinical justification and dose minimization when pediatric imaging using ionizing radiation is indicated.

43052596.title: Geographic and structural factors in brain tumor surgery in Mexico: access, hospital level, and in-hospital mortality in Ministry of Health hospitals.
43052596.author: Cure HW
43052596.abstract:
PURPOSE: Brain neoplasms cause substantial morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries, yet structural and geographic factors in access and outcomes are poorly quantified. Using discharge data from Mexico's Ministry of Health hospitals, we examined access to brain tumor surgery and the relationship between facility level and mortality.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing brain tumor surgery in Ministry of Health hospitals using the national discharge registry (2010-2022). Multivariable logistic regression with hospital-clustered standard errors assessed associations of facility level and travel time with in-hospital mortality, adjusting for clinical and socioeconomic covariates. We also examined timely access among patients and in the population.
RESULTS: Among 10,532 patients, 74.4% reached care within 2 h, and 68.0% of the population lived within 2 h of a Ministry of Health level 3 neurosurgical center, below the 80% Lancet Commission benchmark. Indigenous community, pediatric age, and male sex were associated with lower odds of timely access. Surgery at a level 2 versus level 3 hospital was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (OR 1.25; 95% CI 1.01-1.56; sensitivity range 1.22-1.40), and travel time, less consistently, with a modest increase (OR 1.04 per hour beyond 2 h; 95% CI 1.00-1.07). Malignancy, older age, and pediatric age were associated with higher mortality.
CONCLUSION: Within Mexico's Ministry of Health hospitals, brain tumor surgery is geographically concentrated, and surgery at level 2 hospitals was associated with higher in-hospital mortality. These findings warrant evaluation of level 2 neurosurgical capacity and referral pathways to tertiary centers.

43043512.title: Adapting patient experience measurement to care trajectory in a multidisciplinary brain metastases program: a quality improvement evaluation.
43043512.author: Guterman I
43043512.abstract:
PURPOSE: Patient experience is a core dimension of oncology care quality, but cognitive burden, emotional distress, and complex care trajectories in brain metastases populations may limit traditional survey approaches. This study evaluated the feasibility and interpretability of a locally developed, self-administered patient experience survey administered after initial brain-directed intervention within a multidisciplinary brain metastases program.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective quality improvement evaluation of a patient experience survey administered on tablets at follow-up visits two to three months after initial consultation. Eligible participants were new patients seen in a multidisciplinary brain metastases clinic. Descriptive statistics characterized response patterns, including agreement rates, "not applicable" responses, and missing data. Reasons for non-completion were categorized descriptively.
RESULTS: Among 70 eligible patients, 41 completed the survey (59%). Overall ratings were high, with most respondents reporting that they were always treated with courtesy and respect and always received the best care possible. Communication and decision-making items showed high agreement. Treatment-dependent items showed reduced applicability, including explanations of medication and treatment impact on daily activities, with substantial "not applicable" responses. A subset strongly disagreed with items addressing clarity of results and functional impact. Open-ended responses were generally positive despite structured disagreement.
CONCLUSION: Surveys administered after brain-directed intervention yielded high overall experience ratings but revealed variation in domain applicability, which may reflect treatment exposure and position along the disease trajectory. As a single cross-sectional administration of an instrument without formal psychometric validation, these findings primarily inform survey feasibility and design; trajectory-informed assessment strategies warrant prospective evaluation.

43037779.title: WHO Grade 2 meningioma across three decades: a systematic review with individual patient-level analysis of management and recurrence.
43037779.author: Qiu H
43037779.abstract:
PURPOSE: WHO grade 2 meningiomas demonstrate substantial variability in recurrence risk, with longstanding controversies surrounding postoperative management. We performed a systematic review with individual patient-level survival analysis to characterize management and recurrence across three decades of published clinical experience, interpreted alongside contemporary observational and emerging randomized evidence.
METHODS: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review of PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase was performed. Studies reporting patient-level data for WHO Grade 2 meningioma were included. Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox proportional hazards analyses evaluated progression-free survival (PFS).
RESULTS: Overall, 203 studies comprising 640 patients were included; 337 of 629 patients (53.6%) experienced progression or recurrence. Subtotal resection (STR) was associated with greater progression hazard than gross-total resection (GTR; HR 1.87, 95% CI 1.42-2.45). Adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) following STR was associated with improved PFS (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.21-0.55), persisting in landmark analysis (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.20-0.58). Following GTR, the RT association was less definitive (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.55-1.26). Exploratory analysis did not identify a statistically significant difference in PFS between single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery and fractionated RT (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.30-1.57).
CONCLUSION: This patient-level synthesis characterizes management and recurrence patterns across published literature. Extent of resection remained a key branch point for postoperative risk, with adjuvant RT associated with improved PFS after STR but less definitive results after GTR. Considered alongside contemporary observational and randomized evidence, these findings highlight the value of refining individual recurrence-risk assessment and anticipated treatment benefit to inform more personalized postoperative management.

43037742.title: Inter-lesional heterogeneity and long-term oncofunctional outcomes in multicentric IDH-mutant gliomas treated with single- or multi-stage multisite awake surgery.
43037742.author: Gordon X
43037742.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multicentric IDH-mutant lower-grade gliomas (McLGGs) are rare, and relationships between spatially distinct lesions and long-term oncofunctional management remain poorly characterized. We examined inter-lesional molecular profiles, progression trajectories, and outcomes in patients managed with awake functional-based resection (AFBR).
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 9 patients with 18 IDH-mutated glioma sites treated with multimodal therapy including AFBR. Molecular profiles were classified as concordant or discordant based on IDH mutation and 1p/19q-codeletion status, and progression synchrony as synchronous or asynchronous based on imaging, growth kinetics, progression timing, and anaplastic transformation. Surgical sequencing, treatment response, and functional outcomes were assessed longitudinally.
RESULTS: Nine patients underwent 17 AFBR during a median 7.8-year follow-up. Defining molecular markers were concordant in 5 patients, discordant in 3, and unresolved in 1, while progression trajectories were asynchronous in 6 and synchronous in 3. Multisite and staged resections were tailored to anatomical and functional considerations. An extent of resection ≥ 90% was achieved in 18 of 22 site-level resections (81.8%), with a median extent of resection of 100%. Six patients received temozolomide, with discordant inter-lesional responses in 3. Among the 8 survivors, median KPS at last follow-up was 90 (range: 80-100). Eight patients maintained or resumed professional or academic activity during at least part of their follow-up, while the remaining patient preserved autonomy and social activities. Neuropsychological findings were descriptive and heterogeneous.
CONCLUSIONS: McLGGs displayed heterogenous inter-lesional molecular and progression profiles, with molecular concordance not necessarily translating into parallel growth, histopathological evolution, or treatment response. These findings support a longitudinal approach integrating relative inter-lesional behavior with the evolving oncofunctional context. In this selected series, repeated or multisite AFBR was feasible within individualized multimodal treatment trajectories, with generally preserved long-term functional status.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: N/A.

43035551.title: Stereotactic radiosurgery outcomes in high-grade meningiomas harboring NF2 alterations.
43035551.author: Sahin MC
43035551.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate lesion-level local control and treatment-attributable toxicity after CyberKnife radiosurgery for high-grade meningiomas harboring NF2 alterations.
METHODS: Adults with grade 2 or 3 meningiomas treated with CyberKnife between 2015 and 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Inclusion required tumor sequencing demonstrating a pathogenic or likely pathogenic NF2 alteration and evaluable post-treatment imaging. Integrated central nervous system World Health Organization grade incorporated the 2021 WHO molecular criteria. Time to local progression was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis; exploratory Cox regression accounted for patient-level clustering.
RESULTS: Eleven patients with 19 treated targets were included. All had prior surgery, and 7 (63.6%) had prior radiation. NF2 pathogenic/likely pathogenic alterations occurred in 11 patients; none had confirmed clinical or germline NF2. Median lesion-level imaging follow-up was 48.6 months. Local progression occurred in 9 targets (47.4%). Median time to local progression was 35.4 months; local control at 1, 2, and 3 years was 88.2%, 62.7%, and 47.8%, respectively. Lesion volume > 3 cc was associated with shorter time to local progression (hazard ratio, 4.26; p = 0.025). Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 3 radiation necrosis or post-radiation edema requiring corticosteroids and bevacizumab occurred in one lesion (5.3%); no CyberKnife-related mortality occurred.
CONCLUSION: High-grade meningiomas harboring NF2 alterations showed frequent local progression after CyberKnife, particularly among larger lesions. Severe treatment-attributable toxicity occurred in one of 19 treated-targets. Lesion volume may inform radiosurgical risk assessment, but multicenter validation is needed.

43035531.title: Prior immune checkpoint inhibitor exposure is associated with outcomes after concurrent immunotherapy and stereotactic radiosurgery for melanoma brain metastases.
43035531.author: Fu AY
43035531.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Concurrent administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) with stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is associated with improved outcomes in patients with melanoma brain metastases (MBMs). Prior work suggests concurrent ICI post-SRS may confer additional benefit.
METHODS: Patients aged 18 years or older with MBMs, 4 or more cycles of ICI, and ICI within 4 weeks of SRS from 10 institutions across the United States, Turkiye, and Canada were included in this retrospective study. We examined the associations of concurrent ICI order (before, after, or before and after SRS) and prior ICI exposure with overall survival, local progression-free survival, and distant progression free survival using center-stratified Cox models adjusted for age, Karnofsky-Performance Status, number of metastases, and extracranial disease status. Intracranial progression was additionally analyzed with death as a competing risk.
RESULTS: Two hundred and fourteen patients were included. Thirty-five received ICI before SRS, 125 after SRS, and 54 before and after SRS. Eighty-two (38%) were ICI-naïve. After accounting for prior ICI exposure, treatment order was not associated with any outcome. ICI-naïve status was associated with lower hazards of death (HR 0.62 [95% CI 0.41-0.94]), local progression or death (HR 0.59 [0.41-0.86]), and distant progression or death (HR 0.61 [0.42-0.89]). With death as a competing risk, ICI-naïve status was associated with lower incidence of distant intracranial progression (subdistribution HR 0.55 [0.32-0.91]) but not local progression (subdistribution HR 0.81 [0.51-1.27]).
CONCLUSION: In patients with MBMs receiving concurrent ICI and SRS, prior exposure to ICIs was associated with higher hazards of death and distant intracranial progression.

43035941.title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: A Review in Neuroimaging.
43035941.author: Lohmann P
43035941.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become central to neuro-oncological imaging, impacting clinical and scientific workflows. In clinical practice, AI-based image reconstruction and noise reduction expedite the generation of advanced multiparametric MRI and PET scans. Automated segmentation and volumetric analysis improve reproducibility, speed, and standardization of tumor quantification and response assessment. In research, large language and multimodal models extract structured information from radiology reports and medical records. Collaborative initiatives, such as BraTS and FeTS, have established standardized, privacy-compliant frameworks for large-scale quantitative analyses. Tumor-specific applications include noninvasive molecular profiling in gliomas, grading and recurrence prediction in meningiomas, detection and response assessment in brain metastases, and pediatric-specific modeling aligned with RAPNO. However, AI models remain sensitive to technical and biological variations across institutions, limiting their clinical utility unless appropriate training and validation is performed. Nevertheless, progress is evident in prospective, biopsy-validated infiltration mapping, assessment of resection extent aligned with RANO-Resect, and standardization through AI-RANO. Emerging directions include foundation models, uncertainty estimation, federated learning, AI-enhanced ultra-low-field MRI, and dual-tracer PET. When used as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for the imaging team, AI can increasingly improve the utility, reproducibility, and efficiency of quantitative, multiparametric imaging in patients with brain tumors.

43058222.title: Multicenter characterization of enterocolitis associated with BCMA-directed CAR T cell therapy.
43058222.author: Mikkilineni L
43058222.abstract: Immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis (IEC-EC) is a delayed toxicity of ciltacabtagene autoleucel. The US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium retrospectively adjudicated 54 suspected cases from 8 institutions: 41 were IEC-EC (31 confirmed by anti-camelid variable heavy-chain immunohistochemistry, 10 probable). Through September 2025, cumulative incidence was 3.0% (39 of 1,308 ciltacabtagene autoleucel recipients; 95% CI 2.1-4.1%); 12-month competing-risk incidence was 3.0% (95% CI 2.1-4.1%). Median symptom onset was 75 days after infusion. Grade ≥3 diarrhea occurred in 85% (34 of 40 with diarrhea); 73% (30 of 41) required parenteral nutrition. Despite normal upper endoscopy in 41% (9 of 22), duodenal biopsies showed villous blunting, apoptotic bodies and a dense cytotoxic T cell infiltrate, CD4+ in 61% (19 of 31), CD8+ in 26% (8 of 31) and mixed in 13% (4 of 31). A dominant T cell clone was detected in 76% (13 of 17 tested). Delayed neurotoxicity co-occurred in 41% (17 of 41). At last follow-up, 32% (13 of 41) resolved, 27% (11 of 41) had ongoing symptoms and 41% (17 of 41) died with active IEC-EC. Combined biologic and T cell-directed therapy yielded the highest resolution (55%, 6 of 11) in small subgroups. IEC-EC is potentially fatal and requires systematic evaluation and early directed therapy.

43057233.title: Genomic mediators of acquired resistance to immunotherapy in metastatic melanoma.
43057233.author: Schiantarelli J

43045793.title: Cancer vaccines in the era of immunotherapy: from antigen delivery to immune ecosystem engineering.
43045793.author: Mouren AP
43045793.abstract: Therapeutic cancer vaccines reliably induce tumour-specific immune responses, although translating this immunogenicity into durable tumour control remains a major challenge. This disconnect is probably the result of a series of biological bottlenecks, from antigen selection and presentation to T cell priming, tumour infiltration and resistance to immune suppression. Advances in neoantigen identification, vaccine technologies, immune profiling and computational biology have renewed and re-energized the field. Emerging evidence from clinical trials testing neoantigen-directed vaccines indicates that therapeutic vaccination can improve clinical outcomes particularly when applied in earlier disease settings and integrated within broader immunotherapeutic strategies. In this Review, we examine the mechanisms limiting vaccine efficacy, discuss how they are informing the design of next-generation vaccines, and explore the biomarkers and therapeutic strategies that might enable vaccination to achieve more consistent clinical benefit.

43045674.title: Health-related quality of life in patients with solid cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors: the ARON-MOUSEION-18 systematic review and meta-analysis.
43045674.author: Ciccimarra F
43045674.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) contributes to the value of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), but assessment and reporting remain heterogeneous.
METHODS: This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261330878). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for RCTs of adults with solid tumors comparing ICI-based regimens with non-ICI controls and reporting global HRQoL with the EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL scale or EQ-5D-3L/5L visual analogue scale (VAS). Pooling required a visit-specific adjusted between-group estimate with a 95% confidence interval (CI) or standard error. Random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung-Knapp adjustment) were used. Clinical relevance was assessed using instrument-specific MID benchmarks.
RESULTS: Eighty-two RCTs were included: 42 in the quantitative and 40 in the narrative synthesis, 40 reported EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL, 10 EQ-5D-3L VAS, and 14 EQ-5D-5L VAS. All pooled trials evaluated anti-PD-1-based regimens. The pooled LSMD for EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL was 1.78 points (95% CI 0.71-2.86; p = 0.002; I2 =71.9%). Neither EQ-5D VAS differ significantly. Most trial-level estimates were below the MID, and no trial showed clinically meaningful deterioration. Favorable estimates were concentrated in open-label active-control, advanced/metastatic and lung cancer trials.
CONCLUSION: Anti-PD-1-based therapy results in no clinically important difference in global HRQoL compared with non-ICI controls: the small average advantage is below the MID and concentrated in open-label active-control trials. Interpretation is shaped by trial design, comparator, setting, assessment timing, and incomplete PRO reporting. Standardized PRO reporting is needed across cancer settings and ICI classes.

43044626.title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in surgically resectable hepatocellular carcinoma (PRIME-HCC): a prospective, phase 1b, single-arm trial and translational analyses.
43044626.author: D'Alessio A
43044626.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improves survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. We evaluated this combination as neoadjuvant therapy and investigated its effect on peripheral immunity and the tumour microenvironment.
METHODS: PRIME-HCC is a single-arm, phase 1b trial in adults (aged ≥18 years) with early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A liver function, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1. Patients received nivolumab (3 mg/kg intravenously on days 1 and 22 of the first and second cycle) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg intravenously on day 1 of the first cycle only) before liver resection. The primary endpoint was safety, assessed by treatment-related delays to surgery and adverse events in the intention-to-treat population. Translational analyses included imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics on paired tumour samples, peripheral immunophenotyping, T-cell receptor (TCR) β sequencing, and longitudinal tumour-agnostic circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) profiling. This trial was registered with EudraCT (2018-000987-27) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03682276); follow-up is currently ongoing.
FINDINGS: Between Sept 18, 2019, and Sept 28, 2023, of 43 patients assessed for eligibility, 33 patients were enrolled (25 [76%] male and 8 [24%] female; median age 68 years [range 38-80; IQR 63-73]); median follow-up was 25·7 months (95% CI 21·2-30·1). Any-grade adverse events occurred in 31 (94%) of patients, with treatment-related adverse events (trAEs) in 25 (76%) patients. Grade 3 trAEs occurred in three (9%) patients (transaminase elevation, anaemia, and dyspnoea). Serious adverse events were recorded in three (9%) patients, and no grade 4-5 events or treatment-related deaths occurred. 30 (91%) patients underwent surgery, including two (6%) who had immune checkpoint inhibitor-related surgical delays. Objective response rate by RECIST 1.1 was noted in eight (25%; 95% CI 13-42) patients (one complete response and seven partial responses), with 31 (97%; 84-100) patients achieving disease control. The absence of ctDNA after surgery was associated with improved 2-year recurrence-free survival (nine [82%] of 11 patients vs two [29%] of seven; p=0·049), as was at least 50% ctDNA reduction (median not reached [95% CI not reached] vs 20·9 months [95% CI 16·3-25·4]; HR 0·14 [95% CI 0·02-0·91]; p=0·039). Patients with objective responses showed expansion of peripheral PD-1-positive, Ki-67-positive, CD8-positive T cells (T-responding exhausted cells [Tresp]), associated with higher baseline intratumoral progenitor-exhausted T cells (Tpex) and increased Tresp infiltration. Patients whose disease did not respond to treatment exhibited enrichment of terminally exhausted CD8-positive T cells (Tex-term; CD8-positive PD-1-positive TOX-positive cells) and regulatory T cells.
INTERPRETATION: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab is feasible in early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, and later-phase randomised trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of this treatment strategy. Longitudinal ctDNA monitoring could support detection of minimal residual disease and warrants further prospective validation.
FUNDING: Bristol Myers Squibb, Cancer Research UK, Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro, and Foundation for Liver Research.

43044625.author: Assenat E

43044617.title: Natural ligand-based CAR T-cell therapy targeting BCMA and TACI for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (TriPRIL): a non-randomised, phase 1, first-in-human trial.
43044617.author: Puliafito BR
43044617.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Functional loss of B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) is a recognised mechanism of relapse after BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Targeting multiple tumour antigens simultaneously with a single CAR has the potential to mitigate antigen escape and prolong disease responses. Transmembrane activator and CAML interactor (TACI) and BCMA are both highly expressed on most myeloma cells and bind to the same natural ligand-a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL). We designed TriPRIL, a CAR that uses an engineered trimeric form of APRIL, to target both BCMA and TACI. We aimed to establish the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, and recommended phase 2 dose of autologous TriPRIL CAR T cells.
METHODS: In this first-in-human, open-label, dose-escalation and dose-expansion, phase 1 study, we evaluated TriPRIL in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma at Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, MA, USA). Eligible patients had received at least three previous lines of therapy or had triple-class refractory disease. Previous CAR T-cell therapy and bispecific antibody therapy exposure were permitted. Patients received 3 days of lymphodepletion with intravenous cyclophosphamide (300 mg/m2) and intravenous fludarabine (30 mg/m2) daily on days -5, -4, and -3 before intravenous TriPRIL infusion on day 0. In the dose escalation phase, patients received 1·0 × 108 or 3·0 × 108 TriPRIL CAR T cells to establish the recommended phase 2 dose, which was further evaluated in the dose expansion phase. The primary endpoint was the incidence of study-related adverse events (graded according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5) and dose-limiting toxicities in all patients who received an infusion of TriPRIL CAR T cells, until study completion at 24 months or progressive disease. The data cutoff date was March 24, 2026, when all infused patients had completed at least one assessment of disease response. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05020444), has fully accrued, and is ongoing.
FINDINGS: Between Sept 17, 2021, and Jan 27, 2026, 16 patients were enrolled and underwent leukapheresis, with 15 patients subsequently receiving a TriPRIL cell infusion. Ten (67%) of 15 infused patients were female, five (33%)were male, and the median age was 69 years (IQR 65-75). Nine (60%) of 15 infused patients had previously received BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy, and four (27%) had previously received a BCMA-directed or GPRC5D-directed bispecific T-cell engager. Six patients were treated with 1·0 × 108 CAR T cells, and nine were treated with 3·0 × 108 CAR T cells; there were no dose-limiting toxicities at either dose. The most common adverse events were neutropenia (14 [93%] of 15 patients), nausea (12 [80%]), hypogammaglobulinaemia (eight [53%]), fatigue (seven [47%]), and fever (seven [47%]). Non-haematological adverse events grade 3 or worse occurred in five (33%) patients and all resolved. Cytokine release syndrome (grade 1 or 2 only) occurred in 13 (87%, 95% CI 60-98) infused patients. One (7%, 0-32) patient had grade 2 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and one (7%, 0-32) had grade 2 immune effector cell-associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome; both of these patients had received 3·0 × 108 CAR T cells, and both conditions resolved with corticosteroids. Infections occurred in six (40%, 16-68) infused patients, with a grade 3 infection in one patient (7%, 0-32). There were no treatment-related deaths. The recommended phase 2 dose of CAR T cells was set as 3·0 × 108 cells.
INTERPRETATION: TriPRIL showed a favourable safety profile and warrants further investigation in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, including those previously treated with BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy. The study findings support further development of this dual-targeted, natural ligand-based CAR T-cell approach.
FUNDING: Mass General Brigham and V Foundation.

43043388.title: A comprehensive proteogenomic, immunopeptidomic, and metabolomic atlas decodes immunogenicity in cutaneous melanoma.
43043388.author: Gong J
43043388.abstract: Cutaneous melanoma exhibits strong responses to immunotherapy, yet the system-level mechanisms linking mutational burden, genomic alterations, antigen landscapes, post-transcriptional and post-translational regulation, and immune outcomes remain incompletely defined. We profiled 183 cutaneous melanomas using 13 omic layers, including immunopeptidomics, metabolomics, protein ubiquitylation and glycosylation, to construct a holistic view of tumor immunogenicity. Mass spectrometry-based HLA-I immunopeptidomics revealed correlation between tumor antigens and CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Metabolomics revealed distinct ether-linked lipids and mitochondrial metabolic profiles between primary and metastatic tumors. Ubiquitylomics uncovered a subset of tumors associated with worse survival, characterized by high ubiquitylation of the IFN signaling pathway and ubiquitylation-dependent activation of AKT1. Glycoproteomic analyses identified GPNMB glycosylation as a key feature associated with sex-specific survival, linking this signal to a lysosome-associated program and suggesting potential sex-dependent differences in immunotherapy response. This multi-omic atlas of cutaneous melanoma illuminates mechanisms of immune evasion, informing treatment-relevant patient stratification in melanoma care.

43043383.title: Identification of Proteomic Subtypes with Differential Responses to Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Cutaneous Melanoma.
43043383.author: Chowdhury S
43043383.abstract:
PURPOSE: Predictive biomarkers for combined PD-1/CTLA-4 blockade in metastatic melanoma remain limited. We analyzed pretreatment proteogenomic data to define response and resistance biology.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: We profiled 208 pretreatment FFPE specimens from patients with metastatic cutaneous melanoma treated across 12 institutions, including 164 receiving dual PD-1+CTLA-4 blockade (Discovery, n=97; Validation 1, n=67) and 44 receiving PD-1 monotherapy. Tumors underwent TMT-based proteomics, RNA sequencing, and targeted/low-pass whole-genome sequencing. Pathway clustering, survival modeling, deconvolution, and machine-learning classification defined and validated subtype signatures.
RESULTS: Proteomic pathway clustering identified three reproducible ICI subtypes: immune-enriched ICI-sensitive, ribosome-high, and EMT-like/stromal-enriched. Subtypes stratified progression-free survival after dual ICI in the Discovery (P=0.01) and Validation 1 cohorts (P=0.02). The ICI-sensitive subtype had the highest responder fraction (74% and 73%), compared with ribosome-high (67% and 60%) and EMT-like tumors (44% and 43%) in the Discovery and Validation 1 cohorts, respectively. Subtype-outcome associations were consistent with previous immunotherapy datasets, with pooled hazard ratios ≈0.5-0.8 for immune-enriched tumors. Subtypes plus clinical variables predicted 3-year progression/death better than clinical variables alone in Validation 1 (AUC 0.80 vs 0.64). A 127-protein classifier recapitulated subtype membership in Validation 1 (AUC 0.89-0.97) and predicted 3-year progression/death with AUC 0.79. Subtypes reflected distinct immune, translational, and stromal/ECM programs and nominated POLR3A-associated biology as a candidate resistance axis.
CONCLUSIONS: Proteomic pathway states define reproducible, biologically interpretable melanoma subtypes associated with differential benefit from dual PD-1/CTLA-4 blockade. A clinically tractable 127-protein classifier provides a foundation for prospective biomarker-driven combination immunotherapy trials.

43043005.title: Genomic, Clinical, and Spatial Predictors of Durable Response to BRAF/MEK Inhibition in BRAF-Mutant Melanoma.
43043005.author: Shi Y
43043005.abstract:
PURPOSE: BRAF-targeted therapy (BRAFi/MEKi) and immune checkpoint blockade (anti-PD-1/anti-CTLA-4) have transformed the treatment of BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma. While most patients who respond to targeted therapy eventually progress, a subset derives durable benefit, and biomarkers to identify this subset would inform optimal treatment selection.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: We analyzed pre-treatment tumor samples from a clinically annotated cohort of 155 patients with BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma treated with first-line BRAFi/MEKi and followed for up to five years. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed to derive genomic features, and spatial immunohistochemistry (IHC) characterized the tumor immune microenvironment in a subset of samples. Patients were classified as durable responders (PFS ≥ 24 months) and rapid progressors (PFS < 6 months with progression).
RESULTS: A global metric of tumor genomic heterogeneity, rather than individual gene alterations, distinguished these groups. Combining genomic heterogeneity with baseline tumor burden (e.g., lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) or radiographic lesion dimensions), we developed a parsimonious model that predicted durable responders with high precision and specificity. Notably, the analogous population of patients treated instead with immunotherapy were not durable responders, suggesting that the selected predictors of durable responders are targeted therapy specific. Spatial profiling of the immune microenvironment in a subset of pre-treatment biopsies (n = 47) demonstrated that high intratumoral, but not peritumoral, CD8+ T-cell infiltration predicted prolonged survival on BRAF-targeted therapy.
CONCLUSION/DISCUSSION: These findings highlight the distinct baseline intrinsic and extrinsic features underlying durable response to BRAF-targeted therapy and support their potential implication in guiding treatment selection for patients with BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma.

43048940.title: RE: Matched Targeted Therapy Use after Broad Genomic Profiling in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
43048940.author: Sun M

43043066.title: Longitudinal Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA in Children with Pleuropulmonary Blastoma: A Report from the International PPB/DICER1 Registry.
43043066.author: Schultz KAP
43043066.abstract:
PURPOSE: Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is the most common lung cancer of early childhood. Nearly all PPBs have biallelic DICER1 variants: a loss-of-function allele (often germline) and a second RNase IIIb domain "hotspot" substitution. Except in somatic mosaicism, these hotspots are tumor-specific and ideal liquid biopsy targets.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: For individuals with PPB enrolled in the International PPB/DICER1 Registry, blood samples were collected at timepoints coordinated with clinical venous access. Tumor sequencing identified each patient's RNase IIIb hotspot, enabling personalized droplet digital PCR assays to detect that variant in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).
RESULTS: We analyzed 482 samples from 20 type I and 53 type II/III PPB patients. Among 13 pre-operative type II/III patients sampled pretreatment, 11 (85%) had detectable ctDNA, with tumor size moderately correlated with ctDNA burden (Spearman's ρ=0.574, p=0.051). In contrast, among 8 patients sampled after resection but before chemotherapy, none had detectable ctDNA (p<0.001 vs. unresected). After chemotherapy initiation, ctDNA levels spiked within 1-2 days before rapidly declining. During post-event surveillance, ctDNA was detectable a median of 5.3 weeks before clinical progression (21.7 weeks for negative samples; p=0.001). In type I PPB, DICER1 variants were detectable only in patients with somatic mosaicism.
CONCLUSIONS: In type II/III PPB, ctDNA correlates with tumor size and resection status. The transient rise and fall in ctDNA following initiation of chemotherapy suggests that ctDNA could serve as a real-time in vivo assay of tumor responsiveness, and these findings support further investigation as a pharmacodynamic biomarker for disease response and recurrence detection.

43043010.title: Spatial Immune Organization Associates with Response to CD40 Agonism in BCG-Unresponsive Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer: A Phase I Trial.
43043010.author: Osorio JC
43043010.abstract:
PURPOSE: CD40 agonists activate dendritic cells (DCs) and promote T-cell antitumor immunity, but clinical development has been limited by systemic toxicity and incomplete understanding of determinants of response. In this phase I study (NCT05126472), we evaluated the safety, preliminary clinical activity, and spatial immune correlates of response to intravesical Fc-optimized CD40 agonist 2141-V11 in 25 patients with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG)-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients received weekly intravesical instillations for 3 weeks, with retreatment at weeks 13 and 25 based on disease status. Primary objectives were safety, tolerability, and determination of the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). Secondary endpoints included pharmacokinetics and preliminary clinical activity. Exploratory endpoints including multiplex spatial profiling on tumor specimens to define correlates of response.
RESULTS: Intravesical 2141-V11 was well tolerated, and the MTD was not reached. The RP2D was established at 70 mg. Preliminary clinical activity was observed in 40% of patients, with a median response duration of 20 months. Clinical response was associated with distinct organization of tertiary lymphoid structures, characterized by the presence of DC-CXCL13+ CD4+ and CD8+ T cell triads. Following treatment, responders exhibited decreased proximity between DCs and regulatory T cells (Tregs), whereas non-responders exhibited increased DC-Treg proximity.
CONCLUSIONS: Intravesical 2141-V11 demonstrated a favorable safety profile and preliminary antitumor activity. Spatial profiling revealed immune-cell organizations associated with clinical response, identifying candidate biomarkers and potential strategies for therapeutic combinations. These findings support further clinical evaluation of intravesical 2141-V11 in phase II studies.

43043002.title: Molecular Residual Disease After Definitive Chemoradiotherapy in Locally Advanced Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Value and Optimal Timing for ctDNA Assessment.
43043002.author: Bruixola G
43043002.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Accurate post-treatment assessment after definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-HNSCC) remains challenging due to limitations of standard imaging. We evaluated the diagnostic performance, prognostic value and optimal timing of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for molecular residual disease (MRD) detection.
METHODS: Seventy-four patients with LA-HNSCC treated with definitive CRT were prospectively enrolled. Plasma samples were collected before treatment, at 8 and 12 weeks after CRT, and during follow-up. ctDNA was analysed using a plasma-only methylation-based assay. Diagnostic performance for recurrence detection and associations with progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated and compared with 12-week PET/CT findings.
RESULTS: Baseline ctDNA was detectable in 85.1% of patients. Among post-treatment timepoints, week-12 ctDNA showed the highest diagnostic accuracy for recurrence detection, with 69% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% positive predictive value, and 76% negative predictive value. Detectable week-12 ctDNA was associated with shorter PFS (HR, 6.44; 95% CI, 2.73-16.74; p<0.001) and OS (HR, 7.31; 95% CI, 2.80-22.31; p<0.001 ). Longitudinal ctDNA surveillance identified additional recurrences among patients with initially undetectable week-12 ctDNA. Exploratory analyses integrating PET/CT and ctDNA identified prognostically distinct PFS groups (log-rank P=0.033), with the greatest additional prognostic stratification observed among PET partial-responders.
CONCLUSIONS: Plasma-only methylation-based ctDNA provided high-specificity prognostic information after definitive CRT in LA-HNSCC, particularly at week 12 and in PET partial-responders. ctDNA may complement PET/CT for post-treatment risk stratification, but should not be used as a stand-alone test to exclude recurrence.

43042995.title: Molecular determinants of antibody-mediated priming to enhance detection of ctDNA.
43042995.author: Tabrizi S
43042995.abstract:
PURPOSE: Liquid biopsies can enable cancer detection and monitoring yet remain limited by low amounts of ctDNA. To address this limitation, we previously introduced a monoclonal antibody (mAb) "priming agent" that transiently increased the amount of ctDNA in blood. Here, we investigated the molecular features in both the agent and the target that drive this effect.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: We developed a panel of novel mAbs and other cfDNA-binding agents and characterized their interaction with cfDNA, impact on cfDNA clearance, ability to increase ctDNA recovery, and impact on cfDNA fragmentation and composition in tumor bearing mice.
RESULTS: mAbs targeting either dsDNA or intact mononucleosomes increased the recovery of cfDNA and ctDNA without changing tumor fraction. mAbs with high avidity to dsDNA performed best, highlighting dsDNA as the key structural target for priming agents. One agent preserved short molecules of cfDNA associated with transcription factor binding sites and typically depleted at baseline. The Fc domain was not required for a measurable priming effect, as F(ab')2 retained priming activity. Leveraging these insights, we engineered single-chain agents using the dsDNA binding domain sso7d, expanding priming strategies beyond immunoglobulins.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies the molecular features and general design principles for mAb-based priming agents to enhance recovery and detection of ctDNA.

43057175.title: Beyond cytotoxic chemotherapy: Aspirin and structured exercise to reduce colorectal cancer recurrence.
43057175.author: Sabbagh R
43057175.abstract: Recurrence remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality after curative-intent treatment of stage II-III colorectal cancer (CRC), including among patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy. Recent randomized trials demonstrate that aspirin and structured exercise can further reduce recurrence risk and improve patient outcomes. Two phase 3 randomized trials provide evidence for extending adjuvant strategies beyond cytotoxic chemotherapy in CRC. In ALASCCA, 3 years of low-dose aspirin reduced recurrence by approximately 50% among patients with resected colon or rectal cancer harboring PI3K-pathway alterations, establishing a biomarker-guided approach to adjuvant aspirin therapy. In CHALLENGE, a 3-year structured exercise program initiated after adjuvant chemotherapy improved disease-free and overall survival in patients with resected stage II or III colon cancer. Mechanistically, aspirin may exert antitumor effects through inhibition of cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin signaling, platelet-tumor interactions, and PI3K-related pathways, whereas exercise may act through metabolic signaling, systemic inflammation, and antitumor immunity. Despite distinct anti-tumor mechanisms, both interventions may converge on inflammation, the tumor microenvironment, and immune surveillance. ALASCCA and CHALLENGE trials provide randomized evidence supporting biomarker-directed aspirin and structured exercise as additional adjuvant strategies in patients with CRC. These study findings support testing for somatic PI3K-pathway alterations to identify patients who may benefit from adjuvant aspirin, and support incorporation of structured exercise into survivorship care after CRC resection. Their distinct mechanisms, and potentially complementary biological effects also provide a rationale for evaluating aspirin and exercise in combination.

43050720.title: Real-world anti-EGFR rechallenge in circulating tumor DNA-profiled metastatic colorectal cancer: the REalCHALLENGE study.
43050720.author: Mauri G
43050720.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) rechallenge is a standard therapeutic option for patients with RAS/BRAF wild-type (WT) metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) who benefited from prior anti-EGFR-based regimens. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-guided molecular selection improved efficacy, but routine testing and real-world evidence remain limited.
METHODS: REalCHALLENGE is a retrospective study aiming at assessing the activity of real-world anti-EGFR rechallenge versus other standard-of-care (SoC) treatments in microsatellite stable (MSS), RAS/BRAF WT mCRC patients profiled by ctDNA. The primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR), while secondary endpoints included disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Hyperselection integrating archival solid tissue profiling to ctDNA profiling was also investigated.
RESULTS: 104 patients were included: 69 (66%) ctDNA RAS/BRAF WT and 35 (34%) mutants. Among ctDNA WT, anti-EGFR rechallenge led to higher ORR compared with SoC (29% vs 0%, p = 0.003), and DCR (68% vs 42%, p = 0.049). A trend toward longer median PFS was observed (4.7 vs 2.9 months, p = 0.06), alongside with improved OS (21.9 vs 11.1 months, p = 0.04). In ctDNA mutant patients, outcomes were comparable between groups. In hyperselected non-mutant patients, anti-EGFR rechallenge led to improved ORR (34.4% vs 0%; p = 0.006), PFS (4.98 vs 2.59 months; p = 0.02) and OS (22.20 vs 11.18 months; p = 0.02). No new safety signals emerged.
CONCLUSIONS: Anti-EGFR rechallenge confirmed meaningful activity in ctDNA RAS/BRAF WT MSS mCRC patients in a real-world setting, particularly in a hyperselected population integrating ctDNA and solid tissue profiling. These findings support the value of molecular profiling to optimize selection for anti-EGFR rechallenge.

43062121.title: Targeting Neutrophil Extracellular Traps to Inhibit Colon Cancer Tumor Necrosis and Metastasis.
43062121.author: Gazzara ER
43062121.abstract: Tumor necrosis is associated with poor prognosis in colorectal cancer (CRC) yet is generally viewed as a passive consequence of tumor growth rather than a therapeutic target. We demonstrate that necrosis correlates with metastatic disease in human CRC independently of tumor size. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of primary CRC and colorectal liver metastases revealed that peri-necrotic programs are associated with metastatic progression. Patients with CRC exhibited increased circulating neutrophils, including NET-primed and CD177-low neutrophils with reduced extravasation capacity. Consistent with these findings, intravascular NET aggregates localized adjacent to necrotic regions in human CRC specimens. In a mismatch repair-proficient mouse model of CRC, neutrophil infiltration and NET formation increased during tumor progression, whereas genetic and pharmacologic NET inhibition reduced tumor necrosis, decreased metastasis, and enhanced chemotherapy efficacy. Together, these findings identify NET-driven tumor necrosis as an active promoter of CRC metastasis and support NET inhibition as a therapeutic strategy.

43037074.title: Eligibility and real-world use of adjuvant chemotherapy in colon cancer: a Dutch nationwide study.
43037074.author: Shkurti J
43037074.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adjuvant chemotherapy (ACT) improves survival in patients with resected stage III and high-risk stage II colon cancer, yet its use in routine clinical practice remains variable. Real-world adherence to guideline-recommended ACT and factors influencing treatment use are not well defined at a population level.
METHODS: In this nationwide population-based study, data from the Netherlands Cancer Registry (2005-2020) were used to identify adults with nonmetastatic colon cancer who underwent surgical resection. Eligibility for ACT was defined as pT4N0 or node-positive disease (pT1-3N+ or pT4N+) according to Dutch guidelines and the available NCR variables. Adherence, defined as initiation of ACT when eligible, and factors associated with it were analyzed, including age, comorbidity, tumor characteristics, hospital type and region, and the urgency of the primary tumor resection.
RESULTS: Among 44,471 patients, 22,050 (49.6%) were pathologically eligible for ACT, of whom 12,748 (57.8%) initiated treatment. Among ineligible patients, 2.6% received ACT. Non-adherence was strongly associated with advanced age (29.9% of patients ≥75 without comorbidities received ACT), comorbidity, female sex, right-sided tumors, and non-elective surgery (all p < 0.001). Younger patients were more likely to receive ACT despite pathological ineligibility (p < 0.001). Adherence also varied by hospital type, with lower adherence in teaching and academic hospitals compared with general hospitals (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In this nationwide cohort, guideline-recommended ACT was frequently not delivered to pathologically eligible patients. Adherence was influenced by several patient, tumor and hospital characteristics, highlighting factors associated with variation in guideline-based ACT receipt among colon cancer patients.

43063487.title: The first-in-class SFK 'OFF' inhibitor NXP900 suppresses YAP signaling and demonstrates tumor growth suppression in cholangiocarcinoma.
43063487.author: Kuipers H
43063487.abstract:
PURPOSE: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is an aggressive malignancy with limited targeted therapeutic options and few validated strategies for molecular patient stratification. Src family kinases (SFKs) and YAP signaling contribute to CCA progression, but prior approaches to therapeutically target this axis have shown limited efficacy. Here, we evaluate the preclinical therapeutic potential of NXP900, a first-in-class SFK 'OFF' inhibitor, in CCA.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: The antitumor activity of NXP900 was assessed across CCA cell lines, syngeneic murine models, and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs). Mechanistic studies examined the impact of SFK 'OFF' inhibition on YAP signaling. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses were used to identify molecular features associated with response and resistance.
RESULTS: NXP900 demonstrated decreased tumor cell viability in CCA cell lines and significant tumor growth suppression in PDX models. SFK 'OFF' inhibition suppressed YAP signaling through dual mechanisms involving inhibition of YAP Y357 phosphorylation and activation of Hippo pathway signaling. NXP900 enhanced the efficacy of gemcitabine and cisplatin, supporting its potential use in combination regimens. Multiomic analyses identified enrichment of sensitivity to NXP900 in IDH-mutant CCA models, defining a clinically actionable molecular subset. In addition, resistance to SFK 'OFF' inhibition was associated with activation of an IL13RA2-AKT signaling axis, which was pharmacologically targetable, providing a rational framework for combination strategies.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings establish SFK 'OFF' inhibition with NXP900 as a promising therapeutic strategy in CCA and support biomarker-guided clinical evaluation, including in molecularly defined patient subsets and in combination with standard chemotherapy.
