43046963.title: Low Uptake of Guideline-Recommended MRI Screening for Silent Cerebral Infarcts over the Lifespan in Sickle Cell Anemia.
43046963.author: Hurley G
43046963.abstract: Silent cerebral infarcts (SCIs) are common and clinically consequential in individuals with sickle cell anemia (SCA; HbSS or HbSβ⁰-thalassemia). In 2020, the American Society of Hematology recommended magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based screening in childhood (strong recommendation) and adulthood (conditional recommendation); however, real-world implementation remains poorly characterized. We conducted a multicenter sequential mixed-methods study integrating site-level MRI utilization data, clinician surveys, and semi-structured interviews. Eleven academic SCD programs contributed MRI data for patients aged 5-18 years and >18 years. Clinicians completed the Clinician Guideline Determinants Questionnaire (CGDQ), adapted for pediatric and adult SCI screening, and a purposively sampled subset participated in interviews guided by the Tailored Implementation for Chronic Diseases framework. Thirty-eight clinicians completed surveys, and 25 participated in interviews. Clinicians endorsed the evidence supporting SCI screening; however, readiness to implement adult screening was lower than for pediatric screening (mean CGDQ score 117.0 vs. 126.4). Across 6,959 patients with SCA, fewer than 1 in 8 (11.75%) had undergone brain MRI over the study period (2015-2024), with consistently lower utilization in adult-only programs. Qualitative analysis identified 5 modifiable, multilevel determinants influencing implementation: unclear guideline expectations, patient and family readiness, interprofessional workflows and interpretation capacity, clinic resources and staffing infrastructure, and structural and policy barriers. Despite strong clinician support for SCI screening, implementation remains inconsistent, particularly in adult SCA care. Identified determinants highlight actionable targets for multicomponent implementation strategies to improve uptake and sustainability of MRI-based SCI screening across the lifespan.

43044127.title: Assessing Differences in Timeliness of Emergency Department Pain Treatment for Adult Sickle Cell Pain and Renal Colic.
43044127.author: Gwarzo I
43044127.abstract: The American Society of Hematology (ASH) adopted a site-level quality measure (QM) quantifying differences in median time to first pain medication between adult sickle cell disease (SCD) vaso-occlusive episodes (VOE) and renal colic in emergency departments (EDs). Large-scale evaluation of this QM is lacking. We analyzed records from 103 U.S. adult EDs using 2019-2025 Epic Cosmos electronic health record data. Included sites had at least 100 SCD VOE and 100 renal colic encounters. The QM was calculated per site as median time to first pain medication for SCD VOE minus median time for renal colic, in minutes. Sites were categorized as SCD-Advantaged (<-10 min), Equivalent (±10 min), or SCD-Disadvantaged (>+10 min). Spearman correlations assessed relationships between QM scores and site-level SCD encounter volume, ED length of stay (LOS), and hospital admission rates. Across 103 adult EDs, 436,692 SCD VOE and 5,596,964 renal colic encounters were analyzed. QM scores ranged from -145 to +91 minutes (median: +4). Most sites (56.3%) demonstrated equivalent first-analgesia timeliness; 15.5% provided faster analgesia for SCD VOE, while 28.2% showed delays for SCD VOE (>+10 minutes, median gap: +19 min). QM scores were not associated with SCD encounter volume (p = 0.42), ED LOS (p = 0.94), or hospital admission rate (p = 0.34). We found no major differences in acute pain-care timeliness for SCD versus renal colic across most sites; however, several EDs demonstrated opportunities for improvement. These findings establish the first national baseline for the ASH QM.

43039349.title: Risk factors for antepartum venous thromboembolism in pregnant people with sickle cell disease.
43039349.author: Gerber GF
43039349.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a thrombophilia exacerbated by pregnancy. However, there is not strong evidence for thromboprophylaxis, perhaps because most data addressing pregnancy-related thrombosis in SCD is limited by derivation from administrative datasets. We studied venous thromboembolism (VTE) in a retrospective cohort of pregnant people with SCD who delivered singleton pregnancies at two academic centres between 1990 and 2021. Among 289 pregnancies to 197 SCD subjects, 6% had VTE. We compared characteristics of the first study pregnancy in which a VTE occurred (cases) to the first study pregnancy in subjects without pregnancy-related VTE (controls). Preconception complications associated with VTE were history of VTE (cases: 33% [n = 5/15] vs. controls: 4% [n = 7/182], p < 0.001), acute chest syndrome (ACS) (80% [n = 12/15] vs. 37% [n = 68/182], p = 0.001) and acute care for vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC) in the year before pregnancy (80% [n = 12/15] vs. 43% [n = 70/182], p = 0.006). Prenatal complications associated with VTE were ACS (47% [n = 7/15] vs. 10% [n = 19/182], p < 0.001) and VOC (93% [n = 14/15] vs. 65% [n = 119/182], p = 0.026). Fetal outcomes associated with VTE included gestational age at delivery (median [IQR] 37.0 [34.0-38.1] weeks vs. 38.3 [36.9-39.3], p = 0.004). Studies are needed to establish interventions that attenuate VTE risk and define prophylactic anti-coagulation parameters for this high-risk population.

43067547.title: IMPACT OF HLA B LEADER GENOTYPE ON SINGLE HLA MISMATCHED ALLOGENEIC STEM CELL TRANSPLANTATION: A MULTICENTER COHORT STUDY.
43067547.author: Yucel EE
43067547.abstract:
BACKGROUND: HLA-B leader dimorphism influences HLA-E-mediated natural killer (NK)-cell education and immune regulation and has emerged as a potential determinant of outcomes after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT). However, its clinical significance in contemporary single-locus mismatched unrelated donor (9/10 MMUD) transplantation, particularly in the era of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy), remains incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE(S): To evaluate the impact of donor and recipient HLA-B leader genotypes on transplantation outcomes following 9/10 MMUD allo-HSCT and to determine whether HLA-B leader genotype modifies the effectiveness of different graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis strategies.
STUDY DESIGN: This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 138 adult donor-recipient pairs who underwent 9/10 matched unrelated peripheral blood allo-HSCT for acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, or myelodysplastic syndrome between January 2021 and June 2025 at 20 transplantation centers. HLA-B leader genotypes were assigned using the BLEAT algorithm. Primary endpoints included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), graft-versus-host disease-free relapse-free survival (GRFS), acute and chronic GVHD, grade 3-4 acute GVHD, and day-100 transplant-related mortality (day-100 TRM). Kaplan-Meier, Cox proportional hazards, Gray's test, and Fine-Gray regression analyses were performed together with predefined subgroup, interaction, sensitivity, and false discovery rate (FDR) analyses.
RESULTS: HLA-B leader genotype frequencies were TT in 181 (65%), MT in 85 (31%), and MM in 10 (4%) individuals. The MM genotype was associated with a higher risk of grade 3-4 acute GVHD compared with the TT genotype (Fine-Gray sHR 5.08, 95% CI 1.15-22.40; P=0.032), as well as inferior OS (HR 4.30, 95% CI 1.2-15.7; P=0.025) and a nominally significant association with day-100 TRM (Fine-Gray sHR 4.44, 95% CI 1.09-18.08; P=0.038). Given the sparse events underlying several of these models (events-per-variable 1.3-4.2), minimally-adjusted sensitivity analyses were performed, in which the association with OS did not retain nominal statistical significance. In exploratory analyses, associations between GVHD prophylaxis and outcomes varied according to HLA-B leader genotype. Among TT carriers, PTCy-based prophylaxis was associated with lower acute GVHD compared with ATG-based prophylaxis (sHR 0.41; P=0.017) but not compared with CNI-based prophylaxis on Fine-Gray re-analysis (sHR 0.95, 95% CI 0.50-1.80; P=0.88), whereas no comparable association was observed among MT carriers. After Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the full pre-specified family of 20 primary confirmatory comparisons, none of the nominally significant findings remained significant at q < 0.05 (smallest FDR-adjusted p = 0.156); these associations should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The Turkish cohort demonstrated a high TT genotype frequency (66%).
CONCLUSION(S): HLA-B leader genotype was associated with acute GVHD and survival outcomes after 9/10 MMUD allo-HSCT. Exploratory analyses also suggested differential associations between GVHD prophylaxis strategies and outcomes across HLA-B leader genotypes. These findings warrant prospective validation.

43061586.title: LZTR1 functions as a two-hit tumor suppressor in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
43061586.author: Bonnard AA
43061586.abstract: LZTR1 negatively regulates RAS family proteins via proteasomal degradation. Germline loss-of-function variants cause Noonan syndrome, with emerging evidence implicating LZTR1 in predisposition to childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), though its role in hematopoiesis remains poorly defined. Screening of 1587 children with ALL identified LZTR1 variants in 44 patients (2.8%). Germline variants were detected in 32 patients (2.0%), a frequency comparable to that observed in the general population (1.75%; 1925/110,017; P = 0.50). Somatic LZTR1 alterations were identified in 22 patients (1.4%) and were predominantly bi-allelic, arising through either a germline-plus-somatic or a dual somatic configuration. They persisted at relapse. Despite enrichment in favorable-risk subtypes (ETV6::RUNX1, high hyperdiploid, and ERG/DUX4), bi-allelic LZTR1-mutated cases showed delayed minimal residual disease clearance and higher late relapse risk, identifying a subgroup unsuitable for treatment de-escalation. LZTR1 expression was increased in most wild-type leukemias, consistent with a compensatory response to aberrant RAS pathway activation. Bi-allelic LZTR1 inactivation abolished RAS regulation, leading to deregulated canonical RAS expression and ectopic expression of the non-canonical RIT1 protein, whose involvement in ALL has not previously been reported. These findings establish LZTR1 as a classical tumor suppressor in ALL via a two-hit model. Monoallelic alterations show insufficient signaling perturbation and low germline penetrance, whereas bi-allelic inactivation acts as a driver event linked to a high risk of late relapse despite favorable genomics.

43057679.title: Prospective Multi-Institutional Validation of a Practical Eculizumab Dosing Regimen for Transplant-Associated Thrombotic Microangiopathy in Children and Young Adults.
43057679.author: Jodele S
43057679.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA) is a life-threatening complication following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Terminal complement blocker eculizumab improves outcomes in high-risk complement-mediated TA-TMA, but HSCT recipients exhibit accelerated and highly variable drug clearance, particularly in the presence of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding, making dosing regimens developed for other complement-mediated diseases inadequate. Although individualized dosing using real-time complement biomarker monitoring is effective, these resources are unavailable at most transplant centers, limiting optimized implementation of eculizumab therapy.
OBJECTIVES: The goal of this study was to translate extensive real-time PK/PD-guided eculizumab dosing experience into practical, fixed dosing regimens presented in an easy-to-use table format for HSCT recipients with high-risk TA-TMA, enabling implementation at centers without access to real-time complement biomarker and drug pharmacokinetic (PK) monitoring. We sought to derive weight- and bleeding status-based dosing recommendations for the loading, induction, and maintenance phases of therapy, determine the treatment duration required for most patients, identify dosing schedules with the lowest drug utilization, and prospectively validate this dosing framework in an independent multi-institutional clinical study.
STUDY DESIGN: Eculizumab dosing requirements were derived using PK/PD model-informed simulations integrated with real-time drug concentration, complement biomarker, and clinical outcome data from 64 consecutively treated patients with high-risk TA-TMA (PK64 cohort). Weight- and bleeding status-based fixed dosing regimens were developed for the loading, induction, and maintenance phases of therapy and prospectively validated in an independent multi-institutional interventional study of 23 patients receiving early eculizumab therapy for high-risk TA-TMA with multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (PK23 cohort).
RESULTS: A total of 87 HSCT recipients with high-risk complement-mediated TA-TMA were included. PK/PD modeling identified distinct dosing requirements according to body weight and gastrointestinal bleeding status, established more granular weight categories than currently approved eculizumab dosing, defined phase-specific loading, induction, and maintenance regimens, and identified drug-utilization-optimized dosing schedules with equivalent predicted clinical outcomes. The final product was a set of fixed eculizumab dosing regimens summarized in practical table format for routine clinical use without real-time complement biomarker monitoring. The derived dosing framework was then prospectively validated in an independent, multi-institutional interventional study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03518203; IND 136738; NIH R01 HD093773). Validation confirmed that the derived dosing framework accurately predicted phase-specific dosing requirements, pharmacokinetic behavior, and complement control across independent patient populations, supporting the reproducibility and clinical applicability of the proposed dosing tables.
CONCLUSIONS: This study translates extensive real-time PK/PD experience into practical model-informed fixed eculizumab dosing regimens presented in an easy-to-use table format for HSCT-associated TA-TMA. The framework provides weight-, bleeding status-, and treatment phase-specific guidance that can be implemented at centers without real-time complement biomarker monitoring. It is applicable to eculizumab and eculizumab biosimilars and supports biologically informed treatment discontinuation once complement-mediated disease activity has resolved, helping avoid unnecessarily prolonged therapy.

43057677.title: Autologous Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in Multiple Sclerosis: Key Clinical Questions and Lessons from a Single-Center Experience.
43057677.author: García-Plata MF
43057677.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The HSCT-Mexico program has reported outpatient autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (aHSCT) for multiple sclerosis (MS) using refrigerated non-cryopreserved grafts, split-dose cyclophosphamide, and post-engraftment rituximab.
OBJECTIVE: To provide a critical, question-based synthesis of the program's published experience and identify lessons not covered by its 2021 milestone report.
METHODS: Thirty-two originally supplied institutional publications, one 2025 ASH abstract, and one peer-reviewed 2026 correspondence identified during revision (34 published sources, 2016-2026) were narratively reviewed. Overlapping cohorts were not pooled. Five independent international sources were used for external context.
RESULTS: Across sequential program cohorts, outpatient completion and short-term safety were documented; a 1,700-recipient analysis (1,667 with MS) reported 96.6% fully outpatient procedures, 0.17% 28-day mortality, and 3.3% 28-day morbidity. Approximately 78% had stable or improved patient-reported Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores at 12 months in a 617-person cohort. A 1,438-person ASH abstract found similar favorable EDSS response below and at or above age 60 (75.2% vs 76.9%; p=0.64), but more early complications in the older group (5.8% vs 2.1%; p=0.02). Studies additionally addressed hematologic recovery, toxicity, surveillance, candidate prognostic factors, and patient-centered outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: This synthesis extends the 2021 milestone report through 2026 by explicitly distinguishing overlapping datasets, clinical observations, and exploratory associations. Its strongest evidence concerns program-specific feasibility and short-term safety; efficacy comparisons and generalization, especially in progressive MS, require independent controlled research.

43057676.title: Attainment of Prophylactic Target Posaconazole Concentrations During Admission for Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplant.
43057676.author: Bozaric T
43057676.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) contribute to morbidity and mortality following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Posaconazole is oftentimes utilized for antifungal prophylaxis due to its broad-spectrum activity against yeast and mold. However, oral absorption can be variable and may be influenced by factors such as food intake, gastric acidity, and gastrointestinal function. Although the delayed-release formulation provides more reliable pharmacokinetics, subtherapeutic concentrations are still frequently reported in the HSCT population, especially in patients with mucositis, diarrhea, or poor oral intake. In 2023, Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) transitioned to post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis, which replaced short-course methotrexate. Institutional guidelines now recommend posaconazole for all PTCy recipients, highlighting the need to evaluate antifungal exposure in this population.
OBJECTIVES: The primary objective was to assess the proportion of allogeneic HSCT recipients receiving oral delayed-release posaconazole prophylaxis who achieved an initial prophylactic target trough concentration (≥0.7 µg/mL). Secondary outcomes included time to target attainment, number of levels required to achieve the target concentration, 100-day IFI incidence, and patient-specific factors associated with initial sub-prophylactic posaconazole trough concentrations.
DESIGN: This single-center, Institutional Review Board (IRB)-approved retrospective study evaluated adult patients (≥18 years) undergoing allogeneic HSCT at OHSU from August 9, 2022, through August 9, 2025. The present analysis included patients who received oral delayed-release posaconazole prophylaxis with at least one documented trough level during initial HSCT hospitalization. Baseline characteristics were summarized descriptively. Patient and treatment factors were evaluated as secondary outcomes using the Pearson chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. Analyses were performed using SPSS Software.
RESULTS: Among 105 patients receiving posaconazole, 34 (32.4%) achieved the initial prophylactic target trough concentration, whereas 71 (67.6%) had concentrations below target. Female sex was associated with higher initial target attainment than male sex (43.9% vs 25%; p = 0.043). A total of 98 patients (93.3%) eventually achieved the prophylactic target concentration. The reported median time to target attainment was 16 days (IQR, 7-20 days). Possible but unproven IFIs occurred in 2 patients (1.9%) within 100 days post-transplant.
CONCLUSION: Despite widespread use of delayed-release posaconazole prophylaxis, many allogenic HSCT recipients did not achieve initial prophylactic target trough concentrations; however, the incidence of IFIs remained low. Although routine therapeutic drug monitoring is not recommended in the posaconazole prescribing information, a substantial proportion of allogeneic HSCT recipients in our study had initial trough concentrations below the prophylactic target, with some requiring dose increases to achieve target concentrations. These retrospective findings do not establish whether early therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) improves clinical outcomes. Further research is needed to determine optimal monitoring strategies and whether TDM-guided dose adjustment reduces breakthrough IFIs.

43044128.title: Trafficking Dynamics of Steady State Versus Mobilized Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells in Non-Human Primates.
43044128.author: Fan X
43044128.abstract: The trafficking of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) is central to hematopoietic homeostasis, mobilization, and transplantation, yet its in vivo dynamics remain incompletely understood. Using serial intravascular staining (SIVS) in rhesus macaques, we mapped CD34⁺ HSPC trafficking under steady-state conditions and after CXCR4 antagonist (plerixafor/AMD3100) mobilization. SIVS utilizes sequential infusions of fluorescent anti-CD45 antibodies to label circulating leukocytes, enabling the quantification of blood residence and tissue migration without physiological disruption. Under steady-state, circulating CD34⁺ HSPCs were rare, persisted in blood for less than 48 hours, and minimally re-entered bone marrow (BM) niches. Among extramedullary tissues, the spleen showed the highest HSPC turnover, whereas the thymus and lymph nodes contributed minimally. Plerixafor mobilization induced a rapid, transient surge in circulating CD34⁺ cells that exhibited longer bloodstream persistence and slower egress than steady-state cells, with limited BM rehoming within 12 hours. Bulk RNA-seq revealed distinct transcriptional profiles linked to trafficking behavior. BM-resident HSPCs were enriched for proliferation and stemness signatures, whereas continuously circulating cells showed reduced stemness and enhanced inflammatory signatures. AMD3100-mobilized cells displayed an intermediate transcriptional profile. Together, these findings provide a spatiotemporal framework for understanding HSPC circulation and homing in a translationally relevant non-human primate model. These mechanistic insights can guide the optimization of stem cell mobilization, collection, and engraftment strategies in clinical transplantation and gene therapy.

43039234.title: A multicenter study of allogeneic HSCT in Nijmegen breakage syndrome with conditioning regimen based on reduced doses of treosulfan.
43039234.author: Laberko A
43039234.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nijmegen breakage syndrome (NBS) is a DNA repair disorder characterized by combined immunodeficiency and increased susceptibility to lymphoid malignancies. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is used to cure immunodeficiency and prevent lymphoid malignancies in NBS. Minimal intensity conditioning is an option of choice to prevent HSCT-associated toxicity.
OBJECTIVE: We report a multicenter study of HSCT in NBS using different low dose exposures to treosulfan.
METHODS: 41 patients were included: 16 received treosulfan 30 and 25 - 21 g/m2, all in combination with fludarabine, 24 with cyclophosphamide 20-40 mg/kg. In 25 patients, 9-10/10 matched unrelated, in 10 mismatched related and in 6 matched sibling donor was used. In 19 patients TCRαβ/CD19 depletion, in 15 post-transplant cyclophosphamide (25-80 mg/kg), in 7 patients no T-cell depletion was used.
RESULTS: The median FU time in 33 survivors was 3,5 years (range 0,8-9). OS was 0,81 (95% CI 0,62-1,0) and in 0,77 (95% CI 0,58-0,95) (p=0,77) after treosulfan 30 and 21g/m2 respectively. Deaths, secondary malignancy (n=2, all after treosulfan 30 g/m2) and leukemia relapse (n=4, all after treosulfan 21 g/m2) were considered for events; EFS was 0,75 (95% CI 0,54-0,96) and 0,67 (95% CI 0,46-0,88) (p=0,51) after treosulfan 30 and 21 g/m2 respectively. No patient in either group developed graft failure. No significant differences in incidence of severe organ toxicity, acute and chronic GVHD, viral reactivations and mixed chimerism were observed. OS was 0,91 (95% CI 0,8-1,0) in those who were younger than 8 years of age (n=23) and 0,59 (95% CI 0,33-0,85) in those older than 8 years (n=18), p=0,04.
CONCLUSION: Treosulfan-based conditioning regimen is well tolerated in NBS with no significant differences in HSCT outcomes between those receiving treosuflan 21 or 30g/m2. Two cases of secondary malignancy were observed after treosulfan 30g/m2 and four cases of leukemia relapse after treosulfan 21g/m2. HSCT in NBS should be considered early in life.

43068697.abstract: The diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) requires pathology, posing challenges due to the involvement of deep-seated organs like the pituitary and hypothalamus. We explored the effectiveness US-guided thyroid core needle biopsy (CNB) to a superficial diagnostic approach.

43045775.title: Stem cell source, CD34+ dose and outcomes in haploidentical hematopoietic cell transplantation for myelofibrosis: a study of the Chronic Malignancies Working Party of EBMT.
43045775.author: Czerw T
43045775.abstract: The role of haploidentical hematopoietic cell transplantation (haplo-HCT) in myelofibrosis (MF) remains debated. This EBMT registry-based study included 263 MF patients who underwent haplo-HCT between 2012 and 2020 using peripheral blood (PB; n = 163) or bone marrow (BM; n = 100) grafts. BM was more commonly used in earlier transplant eras and was associated with higher rates of prior splenectomy, myeloablative conditioning, and lower HCT-CI scores. Cumulative incidence of primary graft failure (GF) was higher with BM than PB (12% vs. 4%; p = 0.02), whereas secondary GF at 1 year was similar (8% vs. 10%). Among PB recipients, a higher CD34+ cell dose ( ≥ 7 × 10⁶/kg) was significantly associated (p = 0.009) with faster neutrophil recovery (median 20 vs. 25 days) and higher day-28 engraftment (83% vs. 65%). No such association was observed in the BM group. After a median follow-up of 42 months, 4-year overall survival, progression-free survival, relapse incidence, and non-relapse mortality were 51%, 41%, 23%, and 36%, respectively, with no significant differences between groups. GF remains a major challenge in haplo-HCT for MF, particularly with BM grafts. Higher CD34+ cell doses may improve neutrophil recovery following PB transplantation. Interpretation of long-term outcome comparisons is limited by substantial baseline differences between the study groups.

43057584.title: Comparative analysis of genes encoding hemostatic proteins in human acute promyelocytic leukemia cells and acute myeloid leukemia cells and their murine counterparts.
43057584.author: Zhu XE
43057584.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a distinct subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). APL is associated with a higher incidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation compared with other types of AML. Mouse models can be used to investigate the mechanisms of coagulopathy in APL and AML. However, levels of the genes encoding hemostatic proteins in murine APL and AML cells have not been examined.
OBJECTIVES: To determine if there is overlap in the pattern of expression of genes encoding hemostatic proteins between human APL and AML cells and their murine counterparts.
METHODS: RNA sequencing data from bone marrow or peripheral blood mononuclear cells of 30 patients with APL and 422 patients with AML were obtained from a public database. RNA sequencing was performed on primary murine APL cells isolated from an APL allograft mouse model and the murine AML cell line C1498.
RESULTS: Among coagulation- and fibrinolysis-related genes, the top 3 genes (PLAUR, ANXA2, F13A1) were the same in both human and mouse APL cells. ANXA2 was the top-ranked fibrinolysis-related gene in both human and mouse AML cells. ITGB2 and LPCAT2 were among the top 3 ranked platelet ligand genes in both human and mouse APL and AML cells. However, some highly expressed genes in human cells were not detected in murine cells.
CONCLUSION: Murine APL and AML cells recapitulate the expression pattern of key genes encoding hemostatic proteins observed in human diseases, whereas species-specific differences highlight the need to carefully select pathways for investigation in preclinical models.

43068095.title: A U-shaped association between anti-Xa activity and the composite of major bleeding and thrombosis in adults on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: an exploratory single-center cohort study.
43068095.author: Liu S
43068095.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anticoagulation during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has to hold thrombosis and major bleeding in balance, but the antifactor Xa (anti-Xa) intensity with the lowest combined risk is unknown.
OBJECTIVES: To describe how anti-Xa activity relates to the composite of major bleeding or thrombosis in adults on ECMO.
METHODS: We studied 638 adult ECMO episodes in an exploratory single-center retrospective cohort (2017-2024). The exposure was mean anti-Xa activity over the course of support. Restricted cubic spline logistic regression, adjusted for baseline age, sex, ECMO type, sequential organ failure assessment score, platelet count, and diabetes, modelled the composite of major bleeding or thrombosis between days 2 and 14. We located the risk nadir and a lowest-risk range and examined pre-event and time-updated exposure, competing death, and temporal validation.
RESULTS: Major bleeding, thrombosis, and the composite affected 36.5%, 21.6%, and 50.6% of patients. The adjusted composite risk was U-shaped (P for nonlinearity < .001), with a nadir at 0.40 IU/mL (95% CI, 0.35-0.48) and a derived range of 0.32 to 0.48 IU/mL. Thrombosis fell, and bleeding climbed as anti-Xa rose. Against in-range patients, the adjusted odds ratio was 2.34 (95% CI, 1.63-3.36) above and 1.59 (95% CI, 1.01-2.50) below the range (optimism-corrected 2.24 and 1.60). The U-shape persisted with pre-event and time-updated exposure. In 2022 to 2024, being outside the range derived in 2017 to 2021 was associated with the composite (odds ratio, 1.91; 95% CI, 1.15-3.17).
CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory single-center cohort, intermediate anti-Xa intensity was associated with the lowest combined risk of major bleeding and thrombosis. The data-derived range is hypothesis-generating and needs prospective external validation.

43060538.title: Breaking the ice: cryopreservation of platelets in modern transfusion practice.
43060538.author: Six KR
43060538.abstract: Management of platelet concentrate inventories remains challenging because these products are stored at room temperature and consequently have a short shelf life. In principle, cryopreservation could address this limitation by enabling long-term storage of platelet concentrates. Furthermore, reproducible in vitro studies have demonstrated that cryopreserved platelets are procoagulant, suggesting that they may be more effective at controlling acute bleeding than conventional room-temperature-stored platelet concentrates. However, standard in vitro platelet function assays often fail to capture the full range of platelet function in hemostasis and in general posttransfusion. Clinical studies of cryopreserved platelets in healthy volunteers and patients have largely provided low-quality evidence, including case series, retrospective analyses, or observational studies. Animal studies have provided useful insights into platelet half-life; cryopreserved platelets have been poorly investigated. Recently, the CLIP-II trial reported the results of the first randomized, double-blind clinical trial in patients undergoing high-risk cardiac surgery comparing conventional room-temperature-stored platelets with cryopreserved platelets. This long-anticipated study failed to demonstrate noninferiority with respect to hemostatic efficacy in this patient population. These findings were unexpected given the preserved-or even enhanced-procoagulant phenotype of cryopreserved platelets observed in vitro. This apparent discrepancy highlights the need for more predictive in vitro assays to assess the clinical efficacy of platelet transfusions. The need for improved platelet storage strategies in transfusion medicine remains pressing, underscoring the importance of continued innovation in platelet cryopreservation research. Here, we review current paradigms and highlight key unresolved questions in the field.

43037001.title: Clinical Determinants of von Willebrand Factor Antigen, Activity, and Factor VIII Levels in Transfusion-Dependent Beta-Thalassemia.
43037001.author: Bordbar S
43037001.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Von Willebrand factor (VWF) and factor VIII (FVIII) levels are influenced by multiple physiological and disease-related factors. Patients with transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia (TDT) present a complex clinical setting characterized by chronic anaemia, iron overload, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction, yet data on the determinants of VWF and FVIII in this population remain limited.
AIM: To evaluate VWF antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF:GPIbM, and FVIII activity in patients with TDT and identify their clinical and laboratory determinants.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 180 patients with TDT from an outpatient thalassemia clinic in Shiraz, Iran, were enrolled. Demographic data, ABO blood group, splenectomy status, pre-transfusion haemoglobin, platelet count, and serum ferritin were recorded. VWF:Ag, VWF:GPIbM, and FVIII activity were measured using standard coagulation assays. Independent predictors were identified using multivariable linear regression.
RESULTS: Median VWF:Ag, VWF:GPIbM, and FVIII activity were 121 IU/dL, 121 IU/dL, and 100 IU/dL, respectively. Non-O blood groups were associated with higher VWF:Ag, VWF:GPIbM, and FVIII activity compared with blood group O (p < 0.001). Body mass index independently predicted VWF:Ag, VWF:GPIbM, and FVIII activity. Splenectomy was associated with higher FVIII activity. Platelet count was inversely associated with VWF:GPIbM, whereas pre-transfusion haemoglobin showed an inverse association with FVIII activity. Serum ferritin was not significantly associated with VWF or FVIII levels.
CONCLUSION: VWF and FVIII levels in TDT are influenced by haemoglobin, blood group, body mass index, splenectomy status, and platelet count. These modifiers may complicate the interpretation of haemostatic assays and should be considered when evaluating bleeding disorders in this population.

43037000.title: Validity and Reliability of a Thai Version of the Paediatric Haemophilia Activities List.
43037000.author: Simiwanich S
43037000.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The Paediatric Haemophilia Activities List (PedHAL) is a self-administered instrument for assessing activity limitations in children with haemophilia, yet no Thai version has previously undergone psychometric evaluation.
AIM: To evaluate the validity and reliability of a Thai version of the PedHAL.
METHODS: Following permission from the original developer, the PedHAL was translated into Thai using forward-backwards translation. Content validity was examined via the content validity index (CVI). Construct validity was determined by correlating PedHAL scores with the Functional Independence Score in Haemophilia (FISH) and the Haemophilia Joint Health Score (HJHS). Internal consistency and test-retest reliability were assessed with Cronbach's alpha and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), respectively. The participants were nineteen children with haemophilia who attended the Departments of Rehabilitation Medicine and Paediatrics, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, between June 2021 and September 2022.
RESULTS: The Thai PedHAL demonstrated excellent content validity (CVI = 0.99; threshold ≥ 0.90) and good construct validity, as evidenced by a strong positive correlation with FISH (r = 0.703; range 0.70‒0.89) and a moderate negative correlation with HJHS (r = -0.475; range 0.40‒0.69). Reliability testing revealed excellent test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.955; threshold ≥ 0.90) and excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.944; threshold ≥ 0.90).
CONCLUSION: The Thai version of the PedHAL has acceptable-to-excellent psychometric properties for measuring activity limitations in Thai children with haemophilia. It may serve as a valuable instrument for both clinical and research applications.

43068242.title: Clinical and laboratory-based prognostic factors for pediatric postthrombotic syndrome: findings from the Kids-Duration of Therapy for Thrombosis in Children trial.
43068242.author: Betensky M
43068242.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knowledge on risk factors for the development of pediatric postthrombotic syndrome (PTS) is scarce. We previously identified low plasma fibrinolytic capacity and persistent complete veno-occlusion as candidate risk factors for pediatric PTS. This study aims to substantiate and expand on these findings through a prespecified secondary analysis of the Kids-DOTT trial.
OBJECTIVE: To identify additional clinical and molecular prognostic factors for the development of PTS in children presenting with first time provoked deep venous thrombosis (DVT).
METHODS: We analyzed clinical data and plasma specimens from children with an extremity DVT in the Kids-DOTT trial. PTS was assessed at 1 year post DVT. Plasma fibrinolytic capacity and biomarkers of fibrinolysis were measured in plasma collected at 6 weeks post DVT. Risk factors, identified in our prior work or substantiated in the literature, were evaluated via univariable logistic regression, and variables with P < .05 were included in a multivariable model.
RESULTS: A total of 399 patients were included; 37% developed PTS. In the multivariable clinical model, adolescent age (13 to <21 years) and complete veno-occlusion at 6 weeks were associated with PTS (odds ratio [OR] = 1.69, 95% CI = 1.11-2.57, P = .015 and OR = 2.19, 95% CI = 1.2-3.99, P = .01, respectively). In a biomarker-enhanced model, complete veno-occlusion, reduced plasma fibrinolytic capacity, and increased levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 antigen at 6 weeks were independent prognostic factors for PTS (OR = 2.76, 95% CI = 1.13-6.71, P = .025; OR = 1.83, 95% CI = 1.02-3.30, P = .044; and OR = 1.99, 95% CI = 1.1-3.59, P = .025, respectively).
CONCLUSION: We identified complete veno-occlusion, reduced plasma fibrinolytic capacity, and increased plasma levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 at 6 weeks post DVT as independent prognostic factors for the development of PTS in children with provoked DVT.

43061157.title: Efanesoctocog alfa in mild hemophilia A.
43061157.author: Miesbach W
43061157.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pivotal trials of efanesoctocog alfa enrolled only people with severe hemophilia A; its use in nonsevere disease is limited to mixed-severity cohorts and a single case report of a woman. Mild disease differs: endogenous factor (F)VIII persists, and inhibitor risk is lifelong.
OBJECTIVES: To describe real-world use of efanesoctocog alfa in mild hemophilia A.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective review of consecutive individuals with mild hemophilia A, including symptomatic carriers, treated between October 2025 and June 2026. FVIII activity was measured by a one-stage assay (Actin FSL).
RESULTS: Thirteen individuals (12 men, 1 symptomatic carrier; median age, 56 years; range, 24-86) with baseline FVIII levels of 8% to 57% underwent 17 treatment episodes: 10 perioperative or procedural, 4 on-demand, and 3 prophylactic. Doses of 12 to 37 IU/kg achieved adequate hemostasis in all procedures and bleeds; 3 of 14 (2 varicose vein operations and 1 knee bleed) received a second dose. In 4 episodes, activity was 50% to 72% on days 3 to 4. Prophylaxis was administered at 26 to 40 IU/kg (median, 30) weekly or every 5 days, with trough levels of 33% to 70% (median, 61%). All injections were given on an outpatient basis. FVIII was measured in 7 of 17 episodes. No inhibitors, thrombosis, or hypersensitivity occurred.
CONCLUSION: In this first series dedicated to mild hemophilia A, efanesoctocog alfa, individualized to residual FVIII, provided adequate hemostasis at doses well below the label. A single FVIII measurement on day 3 or 4, using a product-validated assay, may replace routine monitoring. Further observations require prospective study with long-term inhibitor surveillance.

43061140.title: Modeling 1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin response from endothelial storage to individualized dosing in mild hemophilia A and symptomatic carriers.
43061140.author: Buet S
43061140.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Desmopressin (1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin, DDAVP) is the first-line treatment for patients with mild hemophilia A (HA) and symptomatic carriers, but the hemostatic response varies widely. Despite over 4 decades of clinical use, DDAVP plasma concentrations had never been measured in HA, and no mechanism-based pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) model of its hemostatic effects had been developed.
OBJECTIVES: To quantify DDAVP plasma concentrations in mild HA and symptomatic carriers and develop a mechanism-based population PK/PD model linking drug exposure to von Willebrand factor (VWF) and factor VIII (FVIII) responses in order to characterize the sources of variability in DDAVP response.
METHODS: In this multicenter retrospective study, 72 patients (48 males with mild HA, 24 symptomatic carriers) received a single intravenous DDAVP infusion. Plasma DDAVP concentrations were quantified for the first time using a validated liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry method, alongside VWF antigen and factor VIII (FVIII) activity measurements. A mechanism-based population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model was developed using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling.
RESULTS: DDAVP pharmacokinetics followed a 2-compartment model. The pharmacodynamic model incorporated an explicit endothelial storage pool representing Weibel-Palade bodies, from which VWF and FVIII are released upon DDAVP stimulation. FVIII disposition was modeled as a function of VWF-FVIII binding, with distinct elimination rates for free and VWF-bound FVIII. Body weight was the main determinant of DDAVP exposure. Sex, ABO blood group, and age influenced VWF and FVIII baseline levels and disposition. VWF binding doubled FVIII half-life (4.6 vs 2 hours). Female carriers had 54% higher FVIII exposure than males, driven by higher baseline VWF and a longer effective FVIII half-life, resulting in prolonged hemostatic coverage. Simulations reproduced tachyphylaxis through endothelial pool depletion and identified patient profiles at risk of insufficient coverage.
CONCLUSION: This mechanism-based population PK/PD model provides a framework for individualized DDAVP dosing in mild HA and symptomatic carriers.

43036672.title: Rapid measurement of direct oral anticoagulants for clinical decision-making.
43036672.author: Ronchetto E
43036672.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are widely used for the prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disease and have streamlined long-term anticoagulation management due to fixed dosing. However, in time-sensitive clinical scenarios such as acute ischemic stroke, major bleeding, and perioperative care, uncertainty regarding anticoagulant effect can complicate decision-making, such as treatment with thrombolytic and/or reversal agents.
OBJECTIVES: This review summarizes the limitations of existing measurement strategies, outlines key clinical scenarios where rapid assessment may inform care, and evaluates the potential role of point-of-care testing in improving safety and decision-making in hyperacute anticoagulation management.
METHODS: We assessed literature evaluating laboratory and point-of-care methods for assessing DOAC activity, with emphasis on their application in clinical settings, including acute ischemic stroke, major bleeding, and perioperative management.
RESULTS: Current laboratory approaches to assess DOAC activity, including routine coagulation tests and DOAC-specific assays, are limited by variable sensitivity, limited availability, delayed turnaround times, and lack of validated therapeutic thresholds to guide management. As a result, clinicians must make decisions without reliable, timely information on anticoagulant status. Emerging point-of-care technologies offer the potential to address this gap by providing rapid, clinically actionable insights into DOAC presence and effect.
CONCLUSION: Rapid measurement of DOAC activity has the potential to improve clinical decision-making in time-sensitive scenarios involving patients receiving DOAC therapy. Future efforts should focus on integrating these approaches into clinical practice and evaluating their impact on patient-centered outcomes.

43057585.title: A standardised ultrasound strategy safely excludes recurrent deep-vein thrombosis without prior imaging.
43057585.author: Elias A
43057585.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diagnosing recurrent ipsilateral deep-vein thrombosis (DVT) is challenging because current diagnostic strategies often require comparison with prior imaging, which is frequently unavailable in clinical practice.
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether a sequential diagnostic strategy using colour duplex ultrasound with newly developed standardised criteria, and D-dimer testing could safely exclude recurrent DVT without previous imaging.
METHODS: In this multicentre diagnostic outcome study, we enrolled 466 consecutive outpatients with suspected recurrent ipsilateral lower-limb DVT at 27 centres in France. Ultrasound classified findings as acute occlusive/sub-occlusive thrombosis (absence of vein compressibility and flow, or flow outlining the thrombus, no reflux), chronic post-thrombotic changes (partial obstruction, partial compressibility and filling, reflux), or normal. Patients with non-diagnostic (i.e., inconclusive) ultrasound underwent D-dimer testing and, if positive (≥500 ng/mL FEU), repeat ultrasound at day 7±2. Anticoagulation was withheld after a negative strategy result. The primary outcome was the 3-month cumulative incidence of adjudicated symptomatic venous thromboembolism in untreated patients.
RESULTS: Baseline ultrasound was negative in 280 (60.1%), positive in 176 (37.8%), and non-diagnostic in 10 (2.1%). Five patients with non-diagnostic ultrasound had a negative D-dimer and five had a positive D-dimer but unchanged repeat ultrasound. Two patients (0.4%) were lost to follow-up. Among untreated patients with a negative strategy result, symptomatic venous thromboembolism occurred in three patients (1.1%; 95% CI 0.0-2.2).
CONCLUSIONS: The absence of venous occlusion or sub-occlusion on ultrasound safely excluded recurrent ipsilateral DVT without requiring comparison with prior imaging. This approach could simplify diagnostic pathways and overcome a major limitation of current strategies.
