43051620.title: Major Bleeding After Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis for Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Derivation and Transferability of the F-HARP Risk Assessment Model.
43051620.author: Tsaftaridis N
43051620.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an established reperfusion strategy for intermediate- or high-risk acute pulmonary embolism. No validated model exists to predict early major bleeding in this population.
OBJECTIVES: To derive a baseline-only risk assessment model for major bleeding after catheter-directed thrombolysis, and to assess its transferability in an independent cohort.
PATIENTS/METHODS: We pooled patient-level data from 16 cohort studies and randomized trials of catheter-directed thrombolysis for acute pulmonary embolism. The most stable baseline predictors of major bleeding were identified by adaptive LASSO across 1000 bootstrap iterations. Candidate models including 2 to 6 of these predictors were compared on optimism-corrected discrimination and calibration. The selected model was applied to an independent cohort from the RIETE registry.
RESULTS: Of 1246 patients with outcome data and without contraindications to thrombolysis, 75 (6.0%) experienced major bleeding, including 10 intracranial hemorrhages. On internal validation, the F-HARP model (Female sex, Hypertension, Age, high-Risk Pulmonary embolism) showed an optimism-corrected area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.695 (95%CI: 0.639-0.755). In the independent cohort (N=566), patients classified as high risk had higher odds of major bleeding within 30 days than the remainder (11.2% vs. 3.8%; OR 3.18, 95%CI: 1.44-7.05). AUROC was 0.638 (95%CI: 0.519-0.742) and calibration slope 0.630 (95%CI: 0.153-1.107).
CONCLUSIONS: The F-HARP model uses four readily available baseline predictors to identify a subgroup at meaningfully higher odds of major bleeding after catheter-directed thrombolysis. A powered external validation is required prior to its use for precise risk quantification.

43045826.title: European LeukemiaNet clinical signs and symptoms as prognostic markers in polycythemia vera during ruxolitinib.
43045826.author: Palandri F
43045826.abstract: European LeukemiaNet defines the clinical signs and symptoms (CSSs) of polycythemia vera (PV) as progressive splenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, inadequate hematocrit control, and cardiovascular risk factors. In PV patients receiving hydroxyurea, CSSs indicate a phenotype with higher thrombosis risk across the standard risk categories. However, the prognostic value of CSSs for thrombosis or progression to secondary myelofibrosis (SMF) or acute leukemia (AL) during second-line ruxolitinib therapy remains unknown. We assessed the incidence rate ratios (IRRs) of thrombosis and disease progression during ruxolitinib treatment, and the prognostic impact of CSSs at treatment initiation, in 254 PV patients from the PV-ARC multicenter cohort. CSSs were identified in 50.4% of patients, with similar proportions in low- and high-risk groups (50% vs 50.5%). The IRRs for thrombosis and progression to SMF/AL were 1.0 and 4.2 %p‑y, respectively. Conventional thrombotic risk categories did not predict thrombosis or progression. In contrast, CSSs were associated with higher IRRs of both thrombosis (1.8 vs 0 %p‑y, p = 0.05) and progression (6.0 vs 2.3 %p‑y, p = 0.02). Persistent or progressive leukocytosis was the strongest predictor of disease progression. In conclusion, CSSs refine conventional risk stratification by improving prediction of thrombosis and disease progression during ruxolitinib, supporting their integration into routine clinical assessment.

43060557.title: Contemporary management and outcomes of pulmonary embolism during pregnancy: insights from the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team Consortium database.
43060557.author: Ehret J
43060557.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, yet pregnant patients have been excluded from trials defining contemporary PE management.
METHODS: Female patients with acute PE enrolled in the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team Consortium database (2015-2024) were analyzed. Pregnant or postpartum patients (n = 61) were matched 1:3 to nonpregnant female patients (n = 183) by age, body mass index, and European Society of Cardiology risk category. Diagnostic imaging, treatments, and short-term outcomes were compared.
RESULTS: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography was obtained almost universally in both groups (95.0% vs 95.1%, P = 1.00). All patients received therapeutic anticoagulation, with pregnant patients more frequently treated with low-molecular-weight heparin (23.7% vs 8.7%, P = .01). Pregnant patients were more often documented as having contraindications to thrombolysis (44.2% vs 15.4%, P < .01); however, pregnancy or peripartum status was cited as the sole reason in most cases. Use of advanced therapies was comparable (26.2% vs 33.3%, P = .38). Major bleeding (1.6% vs 6.6%, P = .25), in-hospital mortality (1.6% vs 6.0%, P = .31), 30-day mortality (1.6% vs 4.9%, P = .46), and readmission (8.3% vs 12.2%, P = .56) did not differ between groups.
CONCLUSION: Pregnant or postpartum patients with acute PE managed within a multidisciplinary Pulmonary Embolism Response Team framework received diagnostic evaluation, anticoagulation, and reperfusion therapy at comparable rates to matched nonpregnant patients, with no observed increase in major bleeding or short-term mortality. These findings support applying standard risk-stratification and multidisciplinary management to pregnant or postpartum patients with PE, though the study was underpowered for rare outcomes and did not capture fetal outcomes.

43036766.title: Circulating levels of AKT as a marker of high altitude-induced venous thrombosis.
43036766.author: Bhutani A
43036766.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The ascent to high altitude (HA) leads to reduction in partial pressure of inspired oxygen and, thus, culminates in systemic hypoxia. The exposure to HA is now well-established to be an independent predisposition to venous thrombosis (VT; HA-induced VT [HA-VT]). It often occurs in remote terrains, devoid of diagnostic and health care facilities. If left undiagnosed or untreated, HA-VT can culminate in severe clinical outcomes and mortality. Besides caveats in mechanistic understanding, the lack of specific biomarkers constitutes a major limitation for management of HA-VT.
OBJECTIVES: This study sought to establish specific markers of HA-VT, using global proteomics strategy and systematic candidate validation.
METHODS: We used well-established animal models of VT for initial candidate identification. The specificity of the marker was, subsequently, established using samples from patients with clinically established HA-VT besides other HA illnesses (HAIs).
RESULTS: Global proteomics in animal models followed by centrality analysis led to the identification of AKT, whose levels were significantly elevated during hypoxia-induced VT. The clinical relevance of this marker was established by estimating its levels in patients diagnosed with HA-VT. The specificity of marker was established by collecting data for additional markers (soluble intercellular adhesion molecule-1 [sICAM-1], adiponectin, D-dimer, and C-reactive protein)-reported to be associated with pathological hypoxia responses. Our data showed that sICAM-1 (an established marker of endothelial dysfunction) was upregulated in all HAIs (including HA-VT). Both D-dimer and C-reactive protein were upregulated in HA pulmonary edema, HA-VT, and sea level VT, but adiponectin remained unchanged under similar conditions.
CONCLUSION: The circulating levels of AKT were uniquely associated with HA-VT, while sICAM-1 was common to all HAIs.

43065432.title: A bicentric pilot study of apixaban and rivaroxaban quantification using a novel point-of-care system in the emergency department.
43065432.author: Tissier C
43065432.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) do not require routine monitoring; however, rapid assessment of drug concentrations may be needed in critical situations. Laboratory-based anti-Xa assays are recommended but are not consistently available with turnaround times compatible with emergency care.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated analytical performance, agreement at clinical thresholds, precision, and turnaround time of a whole-blood point-of-care (POC) system for measuring apixaban and rivaroxaban.
METHODS: A preliminary laboratory study and a prospective bicentric pilot study in emergency departments were performed on DOAC-treated patients. Paired samples were analyzed using the POC system and a laboratory anti-Xa assay (STA-R Max3; Diagnostica Stago). Agreement within the analytical measuring range (23-200 ng/mL) was assessed using Passing-Bablok regression and Bland-Altman analysis. Concordance at 30, 50, and 100 ng/mL was evaluated using Cohen κ and prevalence- and bias-adjusted κ. Precision and time-to-result were also assessed.
RESULTS: Excellent agreement was observed in both the preliminary laboratory study (r = 0.978; slope = 0.994; median bias = -5.5 ng/mL) and the emergency room study in the 69 analyzed patients (r = 0.965; slope = 1.013; median bias = -10.5 ng/mL). Agreement increased with higher cutoffs (κ = 0.62, 0.89, and 0.94; prevalence- and bias-adjusted κ = 0.83, 0.89, and 0.94 at 30, 50, and 100 ng/mL, respectively). Precision was acceptable (SD ≤ 6 ng/mL; coefficient of variation < 6%). Median time-to-result was shorter with the POC (14 vs 73 minutes).
CONCLUSIONS: The POC system shows a high level of agreement with a laboratory anti-Xa assay and reduced turnaround time, supporting its potential use in the emergency setting.

43068853.title: Acute adverse events associated with commercially available chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell infusions.
43068853.author: Wappler-Guzzetta EA
43068853.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy is increasingly used to treat a variety of diseases, but limited data exist on acute adverse events (AEs) associated with these infusions. We aimed to evaluate AEs associated with Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved CAR-T cell infusions in adult and pediatric patients.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a 5-year retrospective study carried out at a multi-hospital center. Demographic information, disease state, infusion data, medical history, and pre-infusion vitals were extracted from the electronic health record system. Acute AEs were graded per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) criteria. Associations between AEs and collected variables were analyzed using binary logistic regression and machine learning (random forest classifier) methods.
RESULTS: Among 339 adult infusions, 37 AEs were identified (11%): idecabtagene vicleucel 7/40 infusions, lisocabtagene maraleucel 1/39, ciltacabtagene autoleucel 12/104, tisagenlecleucel 5/24, brexucabtagene autoleucel 3/26, and axicabtagene ciloleucel 9/106. Most AEs were grade 1 (54%). Eleven reactions were grade 2, four reactions were grade 3, and two reactions (hypotension, bronchospasm/shortness of breath) were grade 4. No grade 5 AEs occurred. In adults, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) exposure normalized to body weight was associated with a higher acute AE risk (p = 0.007 [binary logistic regression]), supported by machine learning analysis. Among 30 pediatric infusions, one grade 1 hypotensive reaction occurred (~3%). No further statistical analyses were performed in the pediatric cohort because of the limited number of events.
CONCLUSION: FDA-approved CAR-T cell infusions demonstrated a low rate of acute AEs, supporting the safety of current products. The association between increased DMSO exposure and acute AE risk identifies a potential, actionable target for further risk reduction.

43051276.title: Utilization of fresh whole blood for transfusions in remote Japanese islands.
43051276.author: Tanaka A
43051276.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Transfusion therapy is performed at many facilities on remote islands in Japan. However, the availability of fresh whole blood (FWB) and the efficacy of its transfusion on these remote islands remain unclear to date.
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: A survey of FWB use was conducted at 82 facilities on 34 remote islands in Japan where blood products had been supplied between January 2017 and June 2019. Information regarding the transport system of blood products to the facilities, management system for blood donors, and patients who received the FWB transfusions was collected and analyzed.
RESULTS: Nine of the responding 44 facilities were performing FWB transfusions. The median time required for the regular transport of blood products was 7-10.9 h in those nine facilities. The survival rate at 7 days after transfusion was 85% in the 41 patients in whom FWB was transfused. Median blood product use among those patients was 5 units of FWB, 2 units of red blood cells, and 0 units of fresh frozen plasma. Regarding the underlying condition, gastrointestinal diseases were more common in the hospitals without blood product inventories, whereas trauma was more common in those with inventories. The amount of FWB used was significantly larger in the inventory group.
CONCLUSION: FWB was effectively utilized in emergency situations at 20% of the facilities that responded to the questionnaire. It is crucial to optimize the usage of FWB with consideration of the healthcare environment of remote islands.

43045145.title: Analysis of risk factors for perioperative blood transfusion in hip arthroplasty and model construction using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator-logistic regression.
43045145.author: Jin Y
43045145.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Perioperative blood transfusion in hip arthroplasty is associated with increased morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, and higher costs. This study aimed to identify independent risk factors and develop a validated predictive nomogram using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-logistic regression.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective multicenter cohort study enrolled 825 patients undergoing primary hip arthroplasty (January 2020-December 2024) from two Chinese centers. The training cohort (n = 573) and external validation cohort (n = 252) were analyzed. LASSO regression was used for feature selection, followed by multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA).
RESULTS: Perioperative allogeneic transfusion occurred in 148 patients (17.9%). Independent risk factors included age ≥70 years (odds ratio [OR] = 1.84), female sex (OR = 1.52), American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class III-IV (OR = 1.93), coronary artery disease (OR = 1.61), prolonged operative duration (OR = 1.18 per 10 min), lower hemoglobin (OR = 0.72 per 10 g/L), and lower albumin (OR = 0.91 per 1 g/L). Tranexamic acid use was found to be protective (OR = 0.48). The nomogram showed good discrimination in training (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.866, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.812-0.880) and external validation (AUC = 0.816, 95% CI: 0.761-0.873) cohorts. Calibration and DCA confirmed excellent model performance and clinical utility.
CONCLUSION: We developed and externally validated a clinically practical nomogram for predicting perioperative transfusion risk in hip arthroplasty patients. This tool may aid individualized risk stratification, preoperative optimization, and blood management strategies.

43045143.title: Quality indicators for blood transfusion service laboratories: A proposal developed by the Quality Indicators Subgroup of the International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) Quality Management Working Party.
43045143.author: Vuk T
43045143.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Given the diversity of laboratories operating within the blood transfusion service, the Quality Indicators Subgroup of the International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) Quality Management Working Party recognized the need to define appropriate quality indicators for these laboratories, taking into account both shared processes and those specific to each type of laboratory.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Quality indicators in this project are defined for the total laboratory process, and their selection for a particular laboratory is facilitated by indicating the suitability of each individual indicator for each of the three laboratory types: donor-screening laboratories, quality control laboratories, and pre-transfusion testing laboratories.
RESULTS: A total of 35 quality indicators were selected and described (19 in the pre-analytical phase, 6 in the analytical phase, 5 in the post-analytical phase, and 5 in supportive activities). All indicators are presented together with their corresponding numerators, denominators, and the type of laboratory in which their monitoring is considered appropriate.
CONCLUSION: The outcomes of this project are expected to contribute to the harmonization of quality indicators used in transfusion services. The experience gained from the routine implementation of these indicators, along with feedback and suggestions from colleagues, would contribute to their validation and guide the further development of the project.

43039460.title: A new red flag for non-relapse mortality: Prolonged transfusion dependence in acute myeloid leukemia allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant recipients.
43039460.author: Yuan S
43039460.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The hematopoietic cell transplantation comorbidity index (HCT-CI) is widely used to evaluate non-relapse mortality (NRM) risks after HCT. We aimed to evaluate whether the lack of transfusion independence (TI) by Day 30 predicted increased NRM independently of HCT-CI in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) allogeneic (allo-) HCT recipients.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The relationships between HCT-CI, TI, and NRM were evaluated using multivariate analyses in this single-center retrospective study.
RESULTS: A total of 676 AML allo-HCT recipients were evaluated, including 234 (35%) with HCT-CI score ≥3. Median follow-up among survivors (n = 307) was 7.1 years (range: 2.7-11.8). High (≥3) HCT-CI score was significantly associated with increased NRM at 2 years but showed no correlation with attainment of red blood cell (RBC) or platelet (PLT) TI by Day 30. However, the lack of RBC or PLT TI by Day 30 predicted higher NRM independently of HCT-CI. The 2-year NRM incidences were 0.297 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.246-0.350) versus 0.137 (95% CI: 0.105-0.174) for those without or with RBC TI, with adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 2.02 (95% CI: 1.44-2.84, p < 0.001). For those without and with PLT TI, the NRM incidences were 0.374 (95% CI: 0.276-0.471) and 0.179 (95% CI: 0.149-0.212), with aHR of 2.07 (95% CI: 1.30-3.29, p = 0.002). Patients with both high HCT-CI scores and lack of TI by Day 30 had the highest NRM incidence.
CONCLUSION: Lack of TI by Day 30 is an early post-HCT warning sign which predicted increased 2-year NRM independently of HCT-CI and can be combined with HCT-CI to further stratify NRM risks.

43039457.title: Xenotransfusion using red blood cells from genetically modified pigs: Current preclinical research status and clinical application prospects.
43039457.author: Roh J
43039457.abstract: Aging of population and emerging infectious diseases increasingly threaten stable blood supply, underscoring the need for alternative blood sources. Porcine red blood cells (pRBCs) offer notable advantages over human RBCs, including morphological and physiological similarity, established pathogen-free breeding systems, and freedom from ABO- and Rh-compatibility constraints. Recent advances in gene editing have enabled triple-knockout (TKO) pigs lacking the three major xenoantigens recognized by human natural antibodies, reviving interest in xenotransfusion as a potential solution to blood shortages. This narrative review examines preclinical and translational studies on pRBC xenotransfusion, focusing on immunological compatibility, in vivo survival, and adverse reactions across nonhuman primate (NHP) models, genetic engineering strategies, and emerging regulatory frameworks. In Old World NHP studies, TKO pRBCs corrected acute anemia but were cleared within 24-72 h, and retransfusion elicited acute hemolytic reactions from antibody formation. Rapid, multifactorial, immune-mediated clearance of pRBCs remains the principal barrier to clinical use, currently limiting application to emergencies such as acute massive hemorrhage. Future strategies include engineering pigs that express human complement-regulatory proteins and applying immunomodulatory regimens to prolong pRBC survival. Although a dedicated regulatory framework for xenotransfusion is still lacking, recent clearance of pig-organ xenotransplantation trials offers important precedent. Continued progress in genetic engineering and immunosuppression may extend xenotransfusion to emergency medicine and the care of patients with rare blood types.

43039432.title: Active contact strategies to improve return rates in first-time blood donors: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
43039432.author: Silva JPMRJ
43039432.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Retention of first-time blood donors is essential for maintaining a stable blood supply, yet many donors do not return after their initial donation. Active contact strategies, such as text messages and telephone reminders, have been proposed to improve donor retention. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of active contact interventions and to explore whether their effects differ according to communication modality, message content, and timing of delivery.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted. Studies comparing contact interventions with no contact among first-time blood donors were identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library through February 2025. The primary outcome was return donation. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Prespecified subgroup analyses evaluated contact modality, message content, and timing of intervention delivery.
RESULTS: Six RCTs involving 8780 first-time blood donors were included. Active contact interventions significantly increased donor return compared with no contact (RR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.20-1.34). Similar benefits were observed for text messages and telephone calls, with no significant differences between contact modalities. Emotional and reminder-based messages showed comparable effectiveness, as did interventions delivered within 2 months or after 2 months of the initial donation.
CONCLUSION: Active contact strategies are effective interventions for improving retention of first-time blood donors. Their consistent effectiveness across communication methods, message types, and intervention timings supports their integration into donor management programs to strengthen the sustainability of blood supplies.

43039423.title: Iron deficiency in Irish blood donors.
43039423.author: Butler D
43039423.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Blood donation is associated with substantial iron loss, putting blood donors at risk of iron deficiency (ID). Pre-donation haemoglobin (Hb) screening is employed to protect donors from anaemia; however, it does not provide a full picture of iron status. This study aimed to assess serum ferritin levels in Irish blood donors to inform donor iron management strategies.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Residual serum samples from whole-blood and plateletpheresis donations collected by the Irish Blood Transfusion Service in 2022 and 2025 (n = 3857) were anonymised. Serum ferritin was measured using commercially available chemiluminescent immunoassays (Abbott Diagnostics).
RESULTS: Median ferritin concentrations differed by sex, with higher levels in males (61.6 μg/L) compared to females (37.6 μg/L, p < 0.001). Among female donors, ferritin increased by age group. Ferritin concentrations decreased progressively with increasing donation frequency in both sexes. Hb did not vary significantly by donation frequency within each sex. Using a ferritin threshold of <15 μg/L, 9.9% (148/1488) of female donors and 2.9% (49/1678) of male donors were considered iron deficient. ID increased with donation frequency, from 6.5% in females and 0.3% in males on the first donation, to 16.4% and 6.5%, respectively, on the fourth whole-blood donation in 12 months. ID was observed in 3% of male plateletpheresis donors.
CONCLUSION: These results indicate that ID is prevalent among donors who meet Hb eligibility criteria. Sex and donation frequency are determinants of iron store depletion. Monitoring ferritin may be beneficial for early identification of donors at risk of iron depletion.

43063533.title: Winning and Retaining Plasma Donors: A European Collection and Donation Perspective.
43063533.author: Leiße A
43063533.abstract: Most European countries are not plasma self-sufficient and therefore rely on plasma collected in the USA. Expanding the pool of plasma donors and encouraging more frequent donations is essential for achieving self-sufficiency. Incentives can be used by blood establishments to attract or retain donors. This study (N = 2405) examines evaluations of monetary and nonmonetary incentives for plasma donation among nondonors, blood donors, and plasma donors in remunerated (Germany, Austria) and nonremunerated countries (France, The Netherlands). Results reveal substantial differences between remunerated and nonremunerated donation systems. Across donor groups, respondents in remunerated countries (Austria, Germany) expressed a clear preference for financial compensation, which was also associated with the highest plasma donation intentions in both countries. In contrast, preferences in nonremunerated countries were more heterogeneous. While financial compensation was relatively highly evaluated by nondonors and blood donors in nonremunerated countries, existing plasma donors evaluated several nonmonetary incentives similarly or more favorably. Across donor groups and countries, health checks were consistently perceived as one of the most motivating nonmonetary incentives. Furthermore, respondents in nonremunerated countries reported lower motivational orientation toward financial compensation, and plasma donors were more likely to indicate that they would stop donating if compensation were introduced. These findings suggest that financial compensation may be attractive to potential new plasma donors. At the same time, the responses of existing donors highlight the need to investigate whether introducing financial incentives in nonremunerated countries would result in net gains in plasma collection or potential crowding-out effects among existing donors.

43068688.title: Host genetic variation and osteonecrosis during acute lymphoblastic leukaemia therapy: A time-to-event genome-wide association study.
43068688.author: Mikkelsen TB
43068688.abstract: Osteonecrosis (ON) is a debilitating toxicity of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) therapy, but the contribution of common germline variation remains uncertain. We performed a time-to-event genome-wide association study (GWAS) of ON in 1159 European-ancestry children and young adults treated on Nordic Society of Paediatric Oncology and Haematology ALL2008; 63 developed ON during first complete remission. Cox proportional hazard models were adjusted for age, sex and genetic ancestry, with hyperlipidaemia assessed in sensitivity analyses. Candidate loci were evaluated in an independent Associazione Italiana Ematologia Oncologia Pediatrica-Berlin-Frankfurt-Münster (AIEOP-BFM) ALL2000 cohort of 1453 children, including 70 ON cases. Discovery analysis identified genome-wide significant signals near Testis expressed 51 (TEX51) and upstream of glycogen phosphorylase L (PYGL), a gene previously linked to treatment response in childhood ALL. Neither signal showed convincing replication in the validation cohort. Previously reported ON-associated variants and loci also showed no convincing evidence of association in the discovery GWAS, underscoring limited reproducibility across studies. Functional annotation suggested quantitative trait locus effects at the TEX51 locus and regulatory potential for the PYGL-adjacent variant, while exploratory pathway analyses highlighted nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) F2RL1/calcineurin signalling, vascular differentiation, immune receptor signalling, cell-cell adhesion and glycogen metabolism. These findings support ON susceptibility as genetically heterogeneous and identify candidate pathways, particularly NFAT/calcineurin signalling, for future collaborative and functional studies.

43064356.title: Characterization of infections following bispecific T-cell engager therapy in hematologic malignancies.
43064356.author: Huang Z
43064356.abstract: Bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs) have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, but real-world pharmacovigilance data on infection-related adverse events remain limited. This study analyzed data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System from October 2014 to September 2025 for seven FDA-approved BiTEs targeting CD19, CD20, B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA), and G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D). Disproportionality analyses using the reporting odds ratio and Bayesian confidence propagation neural network identified safety signals at the MedDRA High-Level Term (HLT) level. Time to onset and the proportion of fatal outcomes were assessed. Comparisons with chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy were also performed. A total of 3,012 cases (22%) involved infections, with fatal outcomes reported in 33.3% of infection-related reports. At the HLT level, 37 distinct infection-related terms met the prespecified criteria for positive disproportionality signals. These terms included bacterial (n=14), viral (n=12), fungal (n=4), parasitic (n=2), organ-specific (n=3), and other infection-related HLTs (n=2). The median TTO was 36 days (interquartile range 7-124), ranging from 8 days for blinatumomab to 82 days for teclistamab. Bacterial categories showed the earliest median TTO (28 days), followed by fungal and viral categories. Compared with CAR-T, BiTE reported a higher proportion of infections in elderly patients (48% vs 39%) and a longer TTO (36 vs 6 days). Positive infection signals were largely concordant between BiTE and CAR-T. These findings demonstrate a broad spectrum of reported infection-related adverse events, variation in time to onset, and high fatal outcome proportions for certain pathogen-specific categories, highlighting the need for infection surveillance tailored to treatment, timing, and patient risk factors.

43057839.title: CAR-T cells in first relapse of paediatric Down syndrome B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: Oncologist perspectives.
43057839.author: Rubinstein JD
43057839.abstract: Management of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B-ALL) in patients with Down syndrome (DS-ALL) is complicated by increased toxicity and relapse rates. For first relapse of DS-ALL, optimal management is uncertain. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy offers an alternate approach for remission induction and/or definitive curative therapy, and recent reports suggest similar efficacy and tolerability in DS and non-DS patients. We distributed an international survey to paediatric oncologists treating DS-ALL querying opinions on therapy, monitoring and toxicity in this population. Among 89 respondents, 76%, 80% and 64% favoured definitive CAR-T therapy without intent for subsequent haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for early medullary relapse, early and late isolated extra-medullary relapse respectively. For late medullary relapse, 47% preferred definitive CAR-T whereas 51% chose definitive chemoimmunotherapy. Only a minority of respondents selected HSCT as a planned approach for any first relapse: 11%-15% for early relapse; 3%-5% for late relapse. The main perceived benefit of CAR-T therapy was its favourable toxicity profile. Overall, 56% and 77% of respondents felt that it should be considered standard of care for low and high-risk relapse of DS-ALL respectively. Survey responses suggest that developing guidelines to integrate use of CAR-T is warranted for first relapse in DS-ALL.

43057692.title: Long-read nanopore sequencing: A rapid and highly accurate approach for IGHV gene analysis in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
43057692.author: Del Peso Santos T
43057692.abstract: The somatic hypermutation (SHM) status of the immunoglobulin heavy variable (IGHV) gene is a key prognostic and predictive biomarker in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Current methods, including Sanger sequencing and short-read next-generation sequencing, are accurate but have limitations in scalability and turnaround time. Here, we present an integrated workflow for multiplexed long-read nanopore sequencing of full-length IGHV-IGHD-IGHJ rearrangements, leveraging recent advances in sequencing chemistry and base calling. Peripheral blood samples from 60 patients with CLL, representing diverse IGHV subgroups and SHM levels, were analysed. Single-step polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification with EuroClonality-based primers and simultaneous barcoding enabled multiplexing of 12 samples per run. Sequencing on the MinION platform generated over 200 000 high-quality (≥Q30) reads per sample after quality filtering. A dominant productive clonotype was identified in all cases (mean abundance 75%). Comparative analysis demonstrated high concordance with Illumina-based results for IGHV-IGHD-IGHJ gene usage and SHM status. Secondary rearrangements with a frequency of >5% were consistently detected across platforms. The workflow enabled a turnaround time below 24 h at an estimated cost of approximately €70 per sample. In summary, these findings establish long-read sequencing as a rapid, accurate and cost-effective method for full-length IGHV gene SHM assessment, supporting its implementation in routine clinical diagnostics.

43041018.title: Complex karyotype and non-BTK driver mutations associated with BTK inhibitor resistance in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
43041018.author: Mashima K
43041018.abstract: We retrospectively analysed 646 chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) patients treated with Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BTKis) at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute from 2014 to 2023. Among them, 122 underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS) during or at the next office visit after BTKi therapy (ibrutinib [IBR], 85; acalabrutinib [ACA], 23; pirtobrutinib [PIR], 9; vecabrutinib [VEC], 1; zanubrutinib [ZANU], 4). Compared with the non-progressor (NP) group (N = 75), patients with NGS at progression (PD group, N = 47) more commonly had 17p deletion, complex karyotype, heavier prior treatment exposure and prior exposure to a different BTKi before the current regimen. We found 321 mutations in 67 genes, with more mutations in the PD group (231 mutations), including 39 BTK (BTK C481S/F/R/Y, L528W and T474I/L) and 26 phospholipase C gamma 2 (PLCG2) mutations. Among the 12 PD patients with serial samples, all acquired new or expanded BTK or TP53 mutations. Complex karyotype, specifically 8p loss, was significantly enriched in the PD group. tumour protein p53 (TP53), splicing factor 3b subunit 1 (SF3B1), protein phosphatase, Mg2 +/Mn2 + dependent 1D (PPM1D) and notch receptor 2 (NOTCH2) mutations were also significantly more prevalent in the PD group (all p < 0.05). Additionally, pathogenic mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway mutations trended more common and had higher variant allele frequencies (VAFs) in the PD group (p = 0.047). These findings suggest that TP53 aberration and 8p-loss-associated complex karyotype, as well as several non-BTK driver mutations, are enriched in BTKi-resistant patients.

43036868.title: CD20 antigen loss post-venetoclax/anti-CD20 therapy in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: Frequency, characteristics and potential therapeutic implications.
43036868.author: Stewart T
43036868.abstract: Venetoclax plus anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (mAb) regimens have revolutionised treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL); however, CD20 antigen loss is a potential consequence. Given emerging roles for re-treatment with venetoclax plus anti-CD20 mAb and CD20-targeting bispecific antibodies in CLL, we retrospectively assessed the prevalence of CD20-negative CLL in patients treated with fixed-duration venetoclax/obinutuzumab (Ven-O) or venetoclax/rituximab (Ven-R). CD20 expression was assessed by flow cytometry at baseline, end of treatment (EOT) and disease progression, with negativity defined if the log difference in median fluorescence intensity (MFI) between CLL cells and T-cell controls was less than 0.5. Of 60 patients, (34 Ven-O, 26 Ven-R), 6 demonstrated pre-therapy CD20 negativity (1 treatment-naïve, 5 pre-treated) and 10/29 (34%) with measurable residual disease (MRD) at EOT demonstrated post-therapy CD20 loss (4 Ven-O, 6 Ven-R). Notch receptor 1 (NOTCH1) variants were identified in 5/10 (50%) patients with CD20-negative MRD, compared to 3/18 (17%) with CD20-positive MRD and 6/29 (21%) with undetectable MRD. Five patients had longitudinal assessment, with all demonstrating persistent CD20-negative disease long after antibody exposure (follow-up 12-39 months). These results have potential implications for future treatment selection and efficacy.

43048190.title: EHA Guidelines for the use and reporting of patient-reported outcomes in clinical trials of classical Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms.
43048190.author: Oliva EN
43048190.abstract: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are increasingly used in clinical trials of classical Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (Ph-negative MPNs; myelofibrosis [MF], polycythemia vera [PV], and essential thrombocythemia [ET]) as primary, key secondary, secondary, or exploratory endpoints. In the attached COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments (COSMIN) systematic review, patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment was planned or reported in 79 of 87 randomized controlled trials (91%), but PRO results were reported in publications for only 46 of these 79 studies (58%). The review identified 52 reports evaluating measurement properties of 12 PROMs used in classical Ph-negative MPNs. Evidence was uneven. Myelofibrosis Symptom Assessment Form (MF-SAF) v4.0 had the strongest measurement-property evidence for MF symptom burden, with sufficient structural validity and internal consistency with high certainty, but inconsistent findings for reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness. Myelofibrosis Symptom Diary (MPN-SD) had the best content-validity evidence but limited evidence across other properties. MPN-10/MPN-SAF total symptom score (TSS) has substantial clinical-trial experience and clinical familiarity, including use in pivotal development programs, although formal content-validity evidence and some structural and construct-validity findings remain limited or inconsistent. Generic and cancer-specific tools, including European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30 (EORTC QLQ-C30) and EuroQol 5-Dimension instrument (EQ-5D), remain useful for broader health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and health-utility questions but should not be used alone to support MPN-specific symptom claims. These guidelines adapt established oncology PRO standards to MPN-specific instrument, subtype, endpoint, timing, and interpretation issues. They recommend fit-for-purpose PROM selection, standardized self-administration, baseline and longitudinal assessment aligned with trial objectives, prospective missing-data mitigation, sample-size planning for PRO endpoints, and transparent reporting in accordance with CONSORT-PRO and related standards.

43057681.title: Long-term follow-up of relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma patients treated with salvage immunochemotherapy.
43057681.author: Landsburg DJ
43057681.abstract:
BACKGROUND: While the CORAL study demonstrated predictors of survival in patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) large B cell lymphoma (LBCL) following treatment with salvage immunochemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) if demonstrating chemosensitive disease, these findings have not been validated.
OBJECTIVES: To determine risk factors predictive of long-term survival outcomes in a more contemporary cohort of R/R LBCL patients.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective chart review of R/R LBCL patients treated at the University of Pennsylvania from 2008-19 with salvage immunochemothearpy with intent to proceed with ASCT if demonstrating chemosensitive disease.
RESULTS: For the 154 included patients, the overall response rate was 61% and complete response rate 28%. With a median follow up of 104.8 months, the estimated 8 year disease free survival (DFS) was 31% and overall survival (OS) 37%. On multivariate analysis, time to relapse from initial diagnosis <12 months vs ≥12 months was a significant predictor of second occurrence of LBCL and death at 8 years and IPI score ≥3 vs <3 for death at 8 years. Patients with time to relapse from initial diagnosis <6 months (primary refractory) experienced significantly inferior 8 year DFS (12%) as compared to those 6-12 months (32%) as well as those 6-18 months. Findings were similar for 8 year OS. Of all deaths, 7% were due to non-lymphoma causes and 8% of patients developed secondary primary malignancies.
CONCLUSIONS: Time to relapse from initial diagnosis is associated with inferior survival in this cohort of R/R LBCL patients treated with salvage immunochemotherapy, although approximately one-third of patients with early relapse disease achieve prolonged DFS. Additional efforts to risk stratify R/R LBCL patients may lead to more optimal use of this curative treatment.

43048280.title: Fixed-duration glofitamab in patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma: Results from a Phase 1/2 study.
43048280.author: Morschhauser F
43048280.abstract: More effective options are needed to personalize treatment for relapsed/refractory (R/R) follicular lymphoma (FL) by balancing efficacy, safety, and accessibility. We report efficacy and safety of glofitamab, a CD20xCD3 T-cell engaging bispecific antibody, from a Phase 1/2 study in patients with R/R FL after ≥2 prior therapies. Overall, 61 patients were enrolled at the recommended Phase 2 dose of glofitamab (target dose, 30 mg). The overall response rate was 85.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 73.8-93.0), and complete response (CR) rate was 77.0% (95% CI 64.5-86.9). After a median follow-up of 29.3 months, the median duration of CR was 40.2 months (95% CI 20.0-not estimable [NE]). Median progression-free survival was 21.4 months (95% CI 11.4-NE) and the 24-month progression-free survival rate was 49.0%. The most common adverse event was cytokine release syndrome (62.3%; all Grade ≤2). Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome rates were low (6.5%; Grade ≤2, 4.9%; Grade 3, 1.6%). Patients had high rates of undetectable minimal residual disease at their first tumor assessment (Cycle 3) (76.3%), which lasted beyond the end-of-treatment (EOT). Immuno-recovery occurred 12-18 months after EOT in patients with ongoing remission, and T-cell count was not impacted by glofitamab treatment. Fixed-duration glofitamab monotherapy induces durable responses with manageable safety. Glofitamab represents an accessible off-the-shelf therapy for patients with R/R FL, including those with high-risk disease, and an important combination partner for the treatment of R/R FL. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03075696.

43039022.title: Spatial and transcriptomic analyses reveal the adverse prognostic impact of regulatory T cells in follicular lymphoma treated with rituximab-lenalidomide.
43039022.author: Laurent C
43039022.abstract: The prognostic impact of the tumour microenvironment in follicular lymphoma (FL) remains controversial. To adress this, we analysed FL samples from patients enrolled in the rituximab lenalidomide versus any chemotherapy (RELEVANCE) trial using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) and multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). RNA-seq analysis (n = 354) showed that regulatory T-cell (Treg) signatures were associated with shorter PFS in the whole cohort (HR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.01-2.41, p = 0.044), particularly in patients treated with rituximab-lenalidomide (LEN) (R2, HR= 1.84, 95% CI: 1-3.37, p = 0.046) but not with rituximab-chemotherapy (R-chemo, HR = 1.33, 95% CI: 0.71-2.48, p = 0.365). mIF analysis on tissue microarrays (TMA) (n = 394) showed that high infiltration of CD3+/CD4+/FOXP3+ Tregs was associated with shorter PFS in the overall cohort (HR = 1.951, CI: 1.259-3.024, p = 0.0023 log-rank test), particularly in the R2 arm (HR = 2.3, CI: 1.2-4.5, p = 0.0097 log-rank test) and remained significant after FL-International Prognostic Index (FLIPI) adjustment (HR = 1.843; 95% CI: 1.1-2.8, p = 0.006). Whole-slide mIF (WSI) performed in 64 selected cases confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of Tregs in R2-treated patients and further showed that extra-follicular Treg localization was specifically associated with shorter PFS (HR = 2.87, 95% CI: 1.13-7.28, p = 0.020). These data suggest that high Treg infiltration by mIF is associated with inferior outcome in lenalidomide-treated FL patients and may have potential value for risk stratification.

43037011.title: A real-time text-based assessment tool for monitoring symptoms and quality of life for multiple myeloma patients: A feasibility study.
43037011.author: Tellez V
43037011.abstract: Patient-reported outcome (PRO) and quality of life (QoL) assessments for multiple myeloma (MM) patients are traditionally collected at infrequent intervals using burdensome instruments, resulting in limited clinical visibility between visits. This creates a critical gap in care, as evolving symptoms and treatment-related toxicities frequently occur outside scheduled encounters and may remain unrecognized. A single-centre pilot study evaluated the feasibility and clinical utility of a short message service (SMS)-based remote monitoring platform, assessing 8 symptoms and 10 QoL domains for 58 MM patients over 90 days. End-points included feasibility and engagement measured using completion rates, time burden and identification of clinically actionable events. A total of 1604 assessments were delivered, with an overall completion rate of 85.5%, and 72.4% of participants achieving >80% completion rate. Median completion time was 1.80 min. During the 90-day study period, 215 predefined alerts were generated, of which 101 (47.0%) prompted clinical intervention within 48 h, frequently occurring outside routine clinic visits. SMS-based remote monitoring demonstrated high feasibility, sustained engagement and minimal patient burden. This platform enabled real-time identification of symptoms and facilitated rapid follow-up by clinicians, supporting its potential for remote therapeutic monitoring rather than a passive data collection tool.

43057680.title: Predictors of refractory CMV infection in children with haematological malignancies after allogeneic HSCT.
43057680.author: Horton M
43057680.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) remains a major complication of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), yet predictors and immunological consequences of refractory infection are poorly characterised in children.
METHODS: We retrospectively studied 144 children undergoing allo-HSCT for haematological malignancy, assessing predictors of clinically significant CMV infection (csCMVi) and refractory infection, and lymphocyte reconstitution in 107 patients with serial immunophenotyping.
RESULTS: Reactivation occurred in 30% of patients, csCMVi in 27%, of whom 67% met refractory criteria (26/144, 18% of the full cohort). Recipient seropositivity strongly predicted csCMVi (odds ratio [OR] 10.84, 95% CI 4.33-32.14) but was not significantly associated with refractory infection, a comparison limited by the csCMVi cohort being almost uniformly recipient seropositive. Among csCMVi patients, refractory infection was predicted by matched unrelated donor (MUD) (OR 13.00, 95% CI 2.28-101.64) and anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) use (OR 4.59, 95% CI 1.20-19.96). An ordinal donor/ATG gradient showed stepwise increases in refractory risk, from 25% (matched sibling donors) to 88% (MUD with ATG, OR 2.69 per level). Refractory infection was associated with longer viraemia (111.5 vs 14.0 days), higher cumulative viral load, and impaired T-cell reconstitution with lower CD3⁺, CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ counts at day +90 and five-fold lower TEMRA CD8⁺ counts at day +180.
CONCLUSIONS: The transplant factors associated with refractory infection differed from those associated with reactivation, and refractory infection carried a distinct immunological signature, T-cell reconstitution is an accessible biomarker, and TEMRA CD8⁺ expansion warrants prospective evaluation.

43053712.author: Williams S

43050395.title: Endothelial IDO1 Drives BBB Disruption in CAR-T-Associated Neurotoxicity Through KYNU-AA-Wnt/β-catenin Pathway.
43050395.author: Zhang W
43050395.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can cause immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), in which blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption is a central pathological feature, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1)-dependent metabolic reprogramming in cerebrovascular endothelial cells as a mediator linking CAR-T-associated inflammation to BBB dysfunction and neurotoxicity. Patients who developed ICANS exhibited elevated plasma IDO1 activity, a metabolic phenotype recapitulated in a syngeneic CAR-T mouse model characterized by BBB leakage, hippocampal neuronal and synaptic injury, and neurobehavioral impairment. In brain endothelial cells, IDO1 promoted endothelial activation, junctional protein loss, and barrier dysfunction. Pharmacological inhibition and endothelial-specific IDO1 silencing restored barrier integrity and improved neurological outcomes. Mechanistically, IDO1 activation redirected endothelial kynurenine metabolism toward kynureninase (KYNU)-driven anthranilic acid (AA) production, thereby disrupting Wnt/β-catenin-dependent tight junction maintenance. These findings establish the endothelial IDO1-KYNU-AA-Wnt/β-catenin axis as a pathogenic pathway in ICANS and identify endothelial IDO1-dependent metabolism as a potential therapeutic target for preserving BBB integrity and mitigating CAR-T-associated neurotoxicity.

43044881.title: A longitudinal investigation of the financial impact of receiving chimeric antigen receptor t-cell therapy.
43044881.author: Cusatis R
43044881.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Financial toxicity is described as the financial impact of a medical diagnosis. Studies have found that patients undergoing Chimeric Antigen T-cell Therapy (CAR-T) face significant financial impact, but little is known about these experiences over time.
OBJECTIVE: We used mix methods to explore the experiences of CAR-T patients related to financial toxicity in the year after CAR-T.
STUDY DESIGN: This longitudinal, multi-site, mixed-methods study used survey data (5 time points) with a validated measure, the Comprehensive Score for Financial Toxicity (COST-FACIT), and qualitative interviews (4 time points) to examine the financial experiences of patients in the year after CAR-T treatment.
RESULTS: Fifty participants provided survey data. The median COST-FACIT score was 28 at baseline (grade 0, no financial toxicity), 27.5 at 28 days (grade 0), 26 at 90 days (grade 0), 24 at 180 days (grade 1, mild financial toxicity) and 28 at 1 year (grade 0). At each respective timepoint, 37%, 43%, 44%, 52% and 36% of participants had grades 1- 2 of financial toxicity.Eighteen participants completed qualitative interviews. Results aligned with quantitative results, with patients denying major financial impact or describing it in mild or manageable terms. A content analysis identified themes of frustration related to financial impact and insurance uncertainty, gratitude amid adversity, and complexity of factors that influence financial toxicity.
CONCLUSIONS: In this early investigation of the financial impacts on CAR-T recipients, it was clear how unique each patient's experience was based on structural, interpersonal, and individual situations. As the use of CAR-T continues to rapidly expand, understanding the need for tailored and continuous approaches to financial support and resources will be essential when addressing financial toxicity in CAR-T patients.

43043871.title: Cytokines to modulate CAR T cells.
43043871.author: Savoldo B
43043871.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies, but insufficient expansion and persistence, progressive T-cell dysfunction, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments continue to limit durable efficacy and broader application. Cytokines are central regulators of both T-cell fitness and interactions with surrounding immune cells, providing a rationale for incorporating cytokine signals directly into engineered cellular therapies. Here we trace the development and clinical translation of cytokine-enhanced CAR T cells from the pioneering studies with IL-12 to common g-chain cytokines and IL-18. IL-12 established the potential of engineered T cells to deliver potent inflammatory signals locally and mobilize endogenous immunity, but also revealed the risk of systemic inflammatory toxicity. Common g-chain cytokines, particularly IL-7, IL-15 and IL-21, have predominantly been exploited to promote expansion, persistence and favorable differentiation states, with several approaches advancing to clinical testing. IL-18 combines direct support of engineered T cells with recruitment and remodeling of endogenous immune compartments and has recently demonstrated encouraging clinical activity in hematologic malignancies. Emerging strategies increasingly extend beyond cytokine secretion to inducible circuits, synthetic cytokine receptors, unconventional cytokines and combinations of complementary signals. Rational selection of cytokines for specific disease contexts, together with precise spatial and temporal control of their activity, will be critical to balance efficacy against toxicity and realize the full potential of cytokine-engineered cellular therapies.
